自由與監控的拉鋸戰：加州 AB 1856 點燃的全球開源「年齡驗證」阻擊戰
items.summary: 在全球各國政府以「保護兒童安全」為名，逐步將互聯網推向全面監控的浪潮中，開源（Open Source）社群與數碼私隱陣營剛剛在美國西海岸打贏了一場驚險的防守戰。2026年8月底，美國加州參眾兩院一致通過了AB 1856修正案。這項法案被廣大技術愛好者稱為「Linux的免死金牌」，它直接修改了加州先前通過、即將於2027年1月1日生效的《數碼年齡保證法》（Digital Age Assurance Act, AB 1043）。原本的法律強制要求「所有操作系統」必須在用戶開機設置時強制收集年齡，並透過API實時將年齡訊號傳送給第三方App。而最新的AB 1856則明確規定：凡是以GPL、MIT、BSD、Apache等開源許可證分發的操作系統（如Debian、Ubuntu、Fedora、Arch Linux、GrapheneOS等），全部獲得法理解除，豁免於這項強制令。這看似是開源陣營的一場巨大勝利，但在這場席捲全球的「年齡驗證與保證（Age Assurance and Verification）」大戰中，這究竟是一個真正的里程碑，還僅僅是一場短暫且充滿妥協的「小勝」？要理解加州AB 1856的份量，必須先看清全球正在上演的網絡「網絡實名制」變體風暴：-澳洲（Australia）：推行了全球最嚴厲的「16歲以下禁用社交媒體」法案，全面對Instagram、TikTok等平台施加巨額罰款，強制要求其引入生物識別、硬體身分證等手段攔截青少年，並逐步將該框架延伸至AI聊天機器人和遊戲平台。英國（United Kingdom）：隨著《網絡安全法》（Online Safety Act）全面實施，英國通訊管理局（Ofcom）正強制要求所有涉及敏感內容的網站實施「高度有效」的年齡估算，包括人臉年齡估算（Facial Age Estimation）、Open Banking銀行帳戶驗證及信用卡綁定。歐盟（European Union）：透過《數碼服務法》（DSA）與eIDAS數碼身份框架，歐盟正在力推一體化的「歐盟數碼身份錢包（EUDI Wallet）」，試圖透過官方開放源碼的身份驗證工具，將年齡驗證化為加密的「Yes/No」代幣。南美與亞洲：巴西的個人數據保護局（ANPD）同樣在推動將年齡識別責任轉嫁給手機操作系統與應用商店；在這個背景下，加州的AB 1043原本試圖將原本由「個別網站」承擔的驗證責任，直接下沉到電腦和手機的操作系統（OS）底層。-對開源社區與開發者（Existential Threat）：開源軟體的核心是自由、去中心化與匿名。Linux或BSD社區是由全球志願者自發維護的代碼，「Linux沒有總裁，也沒有法務部門」。強迫一個開源操作系統去內置年齡收集API、去對接政府的身份數據庫，在架構上是根本行不通的。開源組織與公司的困境：像Canonical（Ubuntu母公司）或Red Hat等開源商業公司，被迫在合規與開源精神之間拉扯。更致命的是「分叉（Forking）悖論」：由於開源代碼完全公開，即使官方內置了年齡驗證，任何用戶都可以輕易複製一份代碼、把驗證線路删掉（如社群憤怒下揚言要分叉出的Liberated systemd或Ageless Linux運動），這讓開源合規變成了法律上的笑話。-技術內戰：當systemd（多數Linux的核心初始化系統）的維護者試圖在用戶數據庫中加入一個可選的birthDate（出生日期）字段以應對美國各州法律時，社群爆發了毀滅性的輿論海嘯，開發者怒斥這是在向極權合規低頭，將核心組件變成了黑客最愛的私隱「蜜罐（Honeypot）」。組織合力遊說：開源倡議組織（OSI）、FreeBSD基金會等非營利機構聯合向加州立法者發出嚴正警告：不給開源豁免，Linux在加州將走向法理滅絕。這股巨大的輿論壓力，最終逼迫原本強硬的加州議員Buffy Wicks妥協，這才誕生了AB 1856對開源授權（GPL/MIT/Apache等）的全面豁免條款。作為全球頂尖的數碼公民權利組織，電子前鋒基金會（EFF）對年齡驗證的態度是：毫無保留地強烈反對。但同時，AB 1856卻實質上擴大了「年齡網閘（Age-gating）」的覆蓋範圍，進一步將魔爪伸向了網頁瀏覽器和主流商業網站。-網絡匿名制的終結：網民被迫在網絡上「查看證件」，吹哨人、邊緣群體、異見人士將徹底失去保護盾。網絡集權與監控蜜罐：2026年爆出的多宗第三方身份驗證公司（如IDMerit等）數據庫洩漏事件，暴露了數以億計的身份證、人臉識別生物數據被黑客予取予求。邊緣少數群體的數碼孤立：強制驗證迫使平台實施極端的「自我審查」，許多年輕人賴以生存的心理輔導、性教育或少數群體社群（如LGBTQ+援助站），將因為未成年人無法通過高難度驗證（如缺乏信用卡或銀行帳戶）而被徹底切斷。加州AB 1856的全票通過，證明了全球開源社群集體爆發的輿論與技術反叛，確實具備迫使立法者修正瘋狂法案的力量。它為自由軟體保住了一塊不受行政命令干涉的淨土，讓技術人員得以維持一般用途電腦（General-purpose computing）的火種。當四大商業操作系統正式在2027年淪陷、全面開啟年齡API時，大眾視野中的互聯網將不可逆轉地走向分裂與實名化。保護兒童不應以剝奪全人類的私隱為代價，真正的網絡安全，應當如EFF所倡導的——透過嚴格的數據最小化（Data Minimization）和禁止行為追蹤廣告來實現，而不是在每台手機和電腦的底層，裝設一個永遠注視著用戶年齡與面容的「老大哥」眼睛。 請參閱所附表格 ↛

items.title: Transcript: David Booth, Dimensional Fund Advisors founder and chairman
items.summary: The transcript from this week’s, MiB: David Booth, Dimensional Fund Advisors Founder & Chairman, is below. You can stream and download our full conversation, including any podcast extras, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube (video), YouTube (audio), and Bloomberg. All of our earlier podcasts on your favorite pod hosts can be found here. MASTERS IN BUSINESS: David Booth Founder & Chairman, Dimensional Fund Advisors ANNOUNCER : Bloomberg Audio Studios. BARRY RITHOLTZ : This week on the podcast — what can I say? Legendary investor and founder of Dimensional Funds, David Booth, talks about his entire career, his philosophy, philanthropy, how he helped build DFA into a trillion-dollar fund, and why people refuse to just manage what they can and stay calm in the face of volatility and market events. I thought the conversation — and the book, Stay Calm — was fascinating, and I think you will also. David Booth, welcome back to Bloomberg. DAVID BOOTH : Well, thanks for having me. BARRY RITHOLTZ : I was gonna say the same — it’s always a pleasure. I know your background, but I’m gonna assume a lot of listeners may not be familiar with it, so I wanna start by going all the way back to your college and grad school education. You get a bachelor’s in economics from the University of Kansas, then you get a master’s degree focused in business, and then you go to the University of Chicago for a PhD. That very much sounds like academia was the future. DAVID BOOTH : It really was, in the sense that, like a lot of kids, when you’re in college or even high school, you think, boy, I’d like to be a professor — ’cause that’s all you know. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And it’s a great job. You’re on a campus, it looks like fun. DAVID BOOTH : Back in those days, it was a good profession. I mean, there is a thrill of teaching kids, seeing the light go on. Kind of the same thing we have in business, when you have a client and finally — BARRY RITHOLTZ : When they get it. DAVID BOOTH : When they get it, you know, it’s very cool. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So at Chicago, you pivot from a PhD to an MBA, and eventually you become the assistant, researcher, TA to some young professor who was not that much older than you — Gene Fama. Tell us a little bit about what led to that pivot. DAVID BOOTH : Well, the backdrop is, in that period of time — the late sixties, early seventies — that’s when finance really emerged as a science, and it has continued to evolve, even today. by that I mean, for something to be a science, you need testable hypotheses — don’t worry, I’m not getting too heavy into this. before 1960, they just didn’t have the data to test things out. in the early sixties, the University of Chicago developed this research-quality database, CRSP. The CRSP data started in 1926, and they’ve updated it, so now we have over a hundred years of data. BARRY RITHOLTZ : When did Chicago first roll that out? DAVID BOOTH : About ’63. Fama, my mentor and Nobel laureate in 2013, was in the PhD program at Chicago when Jim Lorie and Larry Fisher developed this database, and they turned it over to Gene and said, look, do some papers, do something with this data. he had a head start on everybody, and for the next 20 years he was the most cited academic — BARRY RITHOLTZ : Still one of the most cited academics. DAVID BOOTH : Maybe the most ever, really, in finance. BARRY RITHOLTZ : First mover advantage, for sure. around the time you finish your PhD, Fama’s Efficient Market Hypothesis — that thesis was starting to gain traction, at least in academia, if not yet on Wall Street. Tell us a little bit about what was so attractive about EMH. DAVID BOOTH : Well, it was incredibly exciting. First, let me just make a slight correction — I actually didn’t get a PhD. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Right — you were working on your PhD, and then you got an MBA. eventually I decided the world would be better served if Gene Fama did research and I tried to apply the ideas, rather than the other way around. I walked into his office one day and said, look, I think I’d like to leave the program. he calls up Mac McQuown out at Wells Fargo in San Francisco. Mac was in charge of applying quantitative methods for the bank, and one of the areas he worked on was investing. Mac had always wanted one of his students, so he recommended me, and Mac and I hit it off, and he invited me to come work for them. I decided to leave the program. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So, the first job — did you ever get your MBA, by the way? DAVID BOOTH : I got the MBA on the way out. They gave me an MBA. BARRY RITHOLTZ : That was nice — that was a good investment on their part. You worked for Mac at Wells Fargo, right? I didn’t realize you were on the West Coast for a while. I mean, this is the early seventies, so it was still kind of a Haight-Ashbury kind of thing. Mac is the guy who’s often credited with creating the first version of an index fund. I think, if memory serves, it was for an institutional client’s pension or something like that. DAVID BOOTH : Yeah, right. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Samsonite, that’s right. DAVID BOOTH : It turns out it was really pivotal in the history of finance, for a couple of reasons. One is, in doing all this research in finance, the fundamental question became: if you can’t outguess the market, how are you supposed to invest? Most people grow up thinking — and back in those days, everybody thought — that investing was about trying to pick the next winner stock, and time markets, and that sort of thing. beginning in the mid-sixties, all of a sudden, with this burst of data, they could examine things like: are the professional managers that try to outguess the market worth the cost? they’ve been doing this research for years, and there’s no compelling evidence that they’re worth the cost. I think the most practical assumption for all your readers is that the professional investors don’t seem to be able to beat the market. that has a profound implication. — we can get around to more of the personal story — my parents grew up in the Great Depression and then fought World War II and so forth, and never had much money. they never invested in public markets, ’cause they thought of themselves as outsiders, and the insiders would make all the money and just take advantage of them. they never invested, and they had a little tougher time in retirement than they probably should have. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And to be fair, the history before the post-World War II era was — they weren’t so wrong. DAVID BOOTH : That’s right, they weren’t so wrong. now, that’s the breakthrough. One of the implications of the new science is that the outsiders can do as well as the insiders — maybe better, once fees are considered — ’cause you can buy market portfolios very easily and very inexpensively now, and the pros don’t seem to be able to beat that. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Well, the data on the pros — it doesn’t matter if you’re looking at Morningstar or SPIVA or DALBAR or any of the annual studies — is that in any given year, less than half of professionals beat the index. I think that’s net of fees. DAVID BOOTH : In fact, just yesterday there was a front-page article in The Wall Street Journal — only 27% last year. BARRY RITHOLTZ : In the last 12 months. It was a particularly bad year, because one sector dominated, and if you didn’t have exposure to that sector, you badly lagged. Then the year before, the sector didn’t dominate. you had to pick the sector, time it right, and stay invested. DAVID BOOTH : Of course, if you do all of that, you don’t need our help. BARRY RITHOLTZ : That’s exactly right. Mac creates the first index fund — or one of the first. I’m curious, was there much of a reaction or any pushback from Wall Street, or did it just kind of slip by unnoticed? DAVID BOOTH : No, there was a huge pushback. It was stuff they didn’t want to hear. I mean, they’d been claiming for years — oh yeah, we can beat the market, we can do 15 or 20% regardless of markets — all these claims. It turned out, unfortunately, they couldn’t be backed up by the data. That’s a very powerful lesson in developing arguments: if you have data and the other side doesn’t, it’s kind of an — BARRY RITHOLTZ : Unfair fight. DAVID BOOTH : Unfair fight. it gets into a lot of issues we’ll cover as to why I’m still out trying to deliver that message. BARRY RITHOLTZ : It’s so hard to believe. let’s talk a little bit about that message. You and some of your Chicago classmates — Rex Sinquefield is one, and he had worked on an S&P 500 index fund at American National Bank. then Larry Klotz was also a Chicago — DAVID BOOTH : No — we worked together at A.G. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And that was also in Chicago — in Chicago, but not the university. then Mac basically helped fund this: hey, we wanna apply everything we learned at Chicago and express the insights of Fama in an investible thesis. DAVID BOOTH : And the interesting thing there was that there were really two avenues being explored simultaneously. We had one group that I worked in, and we used as our primary outside consultants Fischer Black and Myron Scholes. BARRY RITHOLTZ : More Nobel laureates. DAVID BOOTH : Two more. It turns out, in working on our project, they developed the Black-Scholes option pricing model, for which Myron became a Nobel laureate — Fischer, unfortunately, had passed away, so he didn’t get it. The idea of our group was: okay, we accept that Michael Jensen and the work of others says these pros can’t seem to beat the market — so what are you supposed to do? By then we’d developed quite a bit of the science, and one idea, based on the models at the time — sounds silly now — was, well, if you have a portfolio that has a higher beta than the market, it should outperform. BARRY RITHOLTZ : What does that mean — you’re just taking on more risk? DAVID BOOTH : You’re just taking on more risk. That’s one way to beat the market: take more risk, but still being diversified. that was the Samsonite account. They figured out a way of creating a higher-beta portfolio. Basically, they would start out with equal positions in all the stocks — they bought equal dollar amounts — and a portfolio like that should have a somewhat higher beta. Let me just refresh people’s memory: the market has a beta of one. if you fluctuate more than the market, you have a beta greater than one, and if you fluctuate less than the market, your beta is less than one. if you have a higher beta, you should outperform — that was the thinking. we were kind of geeky back then. BARRY RITHOLTZ : I think you guys are still a little geeky. DAVID BOOTH : Still — well, yeah, I’ve learned to kind of appreciate that, actually. that was one of the groups. The other group at Wells was the trust department. Mac hired somebody to head up trust investments, and he wanted to do an S&P 500 index fund. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Still early seventies or so? DAVID BOOTH : Yeah, still. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So this is decades before BlackRock, years before Vanguard. This is very, very early. DAVID BOOTH : So that’s what they wanted to do. we go, look, as a scientist, you wouldn’t do an index fund. I think it was some marketing genius who came in and said, no, you want an S&P 500 index fund — everybody can understand that, you can track the index. here again, the pros don’t seem to be able to beat that index, so you can at least get the index return. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Can’t get alpha if you’re not at least getting beta, right? now, those are two different points of view. the reason I emphasize that is that the S&P 500 index fund idea took off. That group left and changed hands a couple of times, and now that’s the cornerstone of BlackRock. BARRY RITHOLTZ : It worked its way eventually to Barclays, and then BlackRock bought that whole business. what are they — 14, 15 trillion, something like that? DAVID BOOTH : No, I mean, it’s phenomenal success. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And they basically proved the point: hey, it’s really hard to beat the market. DAVID BOOTH : Beat the market, yeah. hats off to them. Now, keep in mind — let’s go back to the other group, the one that I was working on that really became the basis for Dimensional. Eventually our group ended up irritating the trust department enough that they got rid of us. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So this was you, Rex — DAVID BOOTH : No, Rex wasn’t there at the time. BARRY RITHOLTZ : He wasn’t? who was the initial group? DAVID BOOTH : Well, Rex was part of the initial group of Dimensional, sorry. we brought people in to help us out — the first two people we talked to were Gene Fama, my mentor, on the research side, and Mac McQuown, who by that time had left Wells as well. Then we pulled together the other leading academics we worked with — people like Merton Miller, the 1990 Nobel laureate, and Myron Scholes, ’97, along with Fama. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So out of all of this, the first fund that you launched when DFA began in Brooklyn was a small cap — or micro cap — strategy. We were the first people to use “small cap” as a term, meaning smaller companies. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And this was based on some of Fama’s initial factors — small seemed to have persistent performance attributes. DAVID BOOTH : Yeah — that was documented about 10 years later. here we are, in some ways flying blind. We had a compelling argument, because in 1981, if you looked at large institutional investors, they weren’t holding the stocks of smaller companies in any meaningful way. if you wanna be diversified, you want large and small, not just large. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So was that the pitch to institutions? Small cap will diversify against the rest of your holdings? we got our first clients with that. we’re off and running with a small cap fund, we had clients, and in talking to Fama, he goes, well, you know, we have a student here that did his PhD dissertation on just what you’re looking at — Rolf Banz. Rolf had done a study breaking down stocks on the New York Stock Exchange into size quintiles, largest to smallest, and the smallest quintile outperformed all the others by quite a bit over time. putting my marketing hat on, I think we’ll define small to be the smallest quintile of companies on the New York Stock Exchange — Mama didn’t raise a complete idiot here, you know. that was how we got started. there really wasn’t a counterargument, ’cause people couldn’t say, oh, I’ve got that covered — they knew they didn’t have small cap covered. what we were able to do is provide access to small companies, and that’s really the basis of Dimensional. about 10 years later, Fama, along with his colleague Ken French, developed this multifactor model. Back when I was at Wells, we just had the single factor, beta. now we had a couple more factors. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So Fama-French started with three, then it was five, and arguably there are just hundreds, most of which are tiny. DAVID BOOTH : Yeah, most of which are tiny. they kind of collapse to — BARRY RITHOLTZ : Five to seven is plenty. DAVID BOOTH : Well, three is plenty. We really have four or five now. you get your big bang out of the first one, the market — BARRY RITHOLTZ : The beta. DAVID BOOTH : The beta. the second factor, say value versus growth — that picks up a lot, not as much as the first. then you get into size — small, that adds a little. Then you can add — pretty soon it’s just diminishing marginal utility, like everything in life. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Quality, momentum — as you work your way down, each generates less and less of a bang. what’s so fascinating to me is nobody had taken the approach that, hey, there is plenty of quantitative data to back this up, here is a testable thesis, a falsifiable thesis, and we can express these ideas in a portfolio. That, to me, was what set the launch of Dimensional apart from everybody else. Am I stating that correctly? DAVID BOOTH : You got it. it shows you how powerful an idea it was, ’cause here we are starting a firm — we have no track record, I’m the first portfolio manager, I’d never managed stocks or even bought stocks before, and we’re operating outta my spare bedroom in downtown Brooklyn Heights. you figure, how can you pull that off? Well, you can pull it off if the idea itself is so profound and backed up with incredible research. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So here’s the key question. Given how powerful that is — but at the time, fairly novel — what do you think Wall Street just missed about index investing? Because clearly there’s a financial opportunity, right? Whether or not your particular fund at the moment is selling performance and active selection, no one else looked at this and said, hey, there’s a business to be had here. DAVID BOOTH : Well, back in those days — and fortunately this is changing now — basically nearly all financial services were distributed through commission salesmen. Wall Street — basically, if you have a commission broker managing your money, I dunno what you’re gonna do, but you’re gonna be trading a lot, I can assure you. if there’s anything that all this research pointed to, it’s that you don’t wanna trade a lot. Trading is a negative expected outcome, kind of like gambling in Vegas. that’s the cornerstone of Wall Street. they go, what do you mean, you’re telling me I shouldn’t be trading a lot? You’re ripping my eyes out. you go, hey, look, all I can tell you is we have logic, reason, and empirical evidence on our side. You have no data — all you have is bluster on your side. over the long haul we’re winning, but it’s taken 50 years. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Hard to make somebody understand something when their income is depending on them not understanding it, to paraphrase. if you don’t have data to support it, then all you’re doing is bluster. look, Wall Street firms in those days were very good at shoving product down people’s throats. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Oh, for sure. I would tell you they’re still pretty good at it. DAVID BOOTH : Well, I’m softening up, because along the way there was a development — an incredible development, almost as important as the development of the science — the fee-only financial advisor, which we started working with in the late 1980s. BARRY RITHOLTZ : We are gonna get to that question. I wanna stay with Fama’s insights and your ability to express them in a portfolio. The fascinating thing about DFA to me is that it’s not simple market-cap-based indexing. The approach that you embraced early on was: how can we express something that’s a combination of what indexing would eventually become, married to a systematic, factor-based investing strategy? by the way, early on, even going back to the days at Wells, we had these two groups — you know, you ought to index — and then the scientists saying, no, you can do better than indexing. that’s 45 years — that’s been our message. As a scientist, you wouldn’t index, for a lot of reasons. One is you’re putting a constraint on yourself: I want to track an index. Constraints cost — in economic terms, that’s costly, and we can get into where the cost is. The other part of it is the silly way that index funds have to behave. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Because of the announcements of additions and deletions — they telegraph it, right? Standard & Poor’s — if they add a new stock into their S&P 500 index today, it’ll go in at tonight’s closing price. If you are an S&P 500 index fund manager, then you want to buy that stock today at tonight’s closing price. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Even though you know it’s gonna run up in anticipation. DAVID BOOTH : Right — and even though you know that every other S&P 500 index fund manager out there is also gonna want that stock at tonight’s close. that’s where — and probably all sciences are this way — there’s the science, and there’s the art of the science. You go to medical doctors, let’s say. They all study the same textbooks; well, some of ’em are just better at execution than others. that’s what we’re talking about here. The simplest of all ideas: if you’re trying to buy a stock at the same time everybody else is, that’s probably not a good trade. Intuition would tell you that. I think our most recent study shows that the runup is about 4% when it goes into the index, the index pays about 4% more than a fair price. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And the flip side is, the deletions have a tendency to outperform the S&P over something like 12 or 24 months. Same thing — people sell in advance, and by the time it’s actually deleted, it’s appreciably cheaper, and maybe that becomes a value. DAVID BOOTH : Well, let me give you the downside of our approach, which is you have to have a certain amount of trust in the manager, because we’re not slavish. I mean, with indexing, you know exactly what they track — the gosh darn index. That’s what they said — that’s all they said they would do. our idea is saying, look, we will use a little flexibility, a little bit of human judgment along the way. Not a lot — not like the old days of wild stock picking — BARRY RITHOLTZ : Throwing darts. DAVID BOOTH : Darts, or whatever. we’ll use a little bit of judgment, and that requires you to have a little confidence in our ability to execute. when we started, a lot of people said, look, how do we know you can execute? Because when you go out and buy or sell, you’re gonna be trading against professional investors. They think they have undiscounted information, if you will — something special, special knowledge — and you don’t. Okay, well, it turns out there’s a flip side to that, which is: if you’re an active manager and you think you know something special, you also realize the half-life of that is really short. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Today it’s probably milliseconds. DAVID BOOTH : Probably milliseconds. if you wanna get rid of a stock, you want to get rid of it right now — at least by the end of the day. we come along, and we’re kind of indifferent. We buy 10,000 stocks — you know, on any given day, we don’t buy all 10,000 of ’em. We focus a lot on what’s trading easily that day. Even a small company stock, 20% of the time it trades a lot. BARRY RITHOLTZ : In other words, you can use execution and volatility as a source of better pricing. DAVID BOOTH : Better pricing, yeah. that’s worked out over 45 years — the first 45 are the toughest, I realize. still, people slap their forehead — that’s hard to believe, that there’s this professional money manager out there trading against you. It’s not that we take advantage of them. We provide liquidity, and our clients get the benefit of providing that service. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And by providing liquidity, it means you’re willing to be a buyer at times when many other people are not. DAVID BOOTH : But we’re not gonna pay retail for that stock. I mean — if you can talk to me, can you do something for me on the price? BARRY RITHOLTZ : Take a little something off. Coming up, we continue our conversation with David Booth, founder and chairman of Dimensional Fund Advisors, talking about his brand-new book, Stay Calm: Learning to Embrace Uncertainty in Investing and Life. You’re listening to Masters in Business on Bloomberg Radio. My extra special guest today is David Booth. His new book is out — probably by the time you’re hearing this — Stay Calm: Learning to Embrace Uncertainty in Investing and Life. I wanna sum up the book in a sentence, and then we’re gonna really delve into it: “Uncertainty isn’t something to fear — it’s where possibility lives.” Ooh. DAVID BOOTH : That is a good question. Every now and then, you know, you write something down — BARRY RITHOLTZ : By the way, I have a dozen fantastic quotes, and I’m gonna try and click through all of them. DAVID BOOTH : No, it’s funny, ’cause you write it, and then you forget you wrote it, and then you go back and look at it and go, hey — BARRY RITHOLTZ : That’s not bad. DAVID BOOTH : That’s not bad, yeah. let me tell you about a breakthrough that happened to us about 10 years ago. We realized that there are a lot of parallels between investing and your life experiences, and a lot of that has to deal with how you deal with uncertainty. You know, as you grow, you learn how to deal with uncertainty, and what you realize is uncertainty is what creates opportunity. If there were no uncertainty, you wouldn’t have the ability to progress. it’s not about eliminating uncertainty — it’s about managing uncertainty. That’s true in life, and the reason I bring that up is ’cause that’s also true in investing. If there were no uncertainty — in other words, if all investing was riskless — BARRY RITHOLTZ : I got some 10-year Treasuries at three and a half percent that you can hold and barely keep up with inflation. DAVID BOOTH : Well, if there were no uncertainty in investing, every investment would have the same return — the riskless return, whatever that is. in investing as well, it’s uncertainty that creates opportunity. once people start to realize that, we go — let’s go back: how do you deal with uncertainty? Well, first off, you realize that life is not totally predictable. I mean, think back 20 years ago. Could you have predicted where you are today, or where you’ll be 20 years from now? BARRY RITHOLTZ : Nobody in December 2019 was predicting a pandemic the next year — in a market that would scream higher. You could show it in every annual forecast we see — and we’ll talk a little bit about predictions in a minute — but the future is inherently unknowable. DAVID BOOTH : And so embrace that uncertainty. That’s what gives us the opportunity in life and investing. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So what do you say to people who are investors — hey, uncertainty creates opportunity — but how does the average mom-and-pop investor live through the regular 15, 20, 25% drawdowns we see all the time in equity markets? DAVID BOOTH : Well, the quick answer to that is stay calm — that’s why we call it that; it’s the name of the book. let me give you an example of the fundamental problem we have with helping people stay invested. Let’s say bad news comes into the market — the pandemic, or a particular stock. then you look at the stock or the market and you see it’s down 20% or whatever, and you go, holy cow, I gotta get out. There’s bad news and the market and things are dropping — that is human nature. What we’d like to have people think is: look, okay, the pandemic — bad news — came into the market, and the market’s down 20 or 30%. people were saying, what are we supposed to do? What do you think is gonna happen? I go, hey, look, I don’t know what’s gonna happen — and anybody that thinks they can predict what’s gonna happen, I’d be a little suspicious about. here’s what I believe will happen: people aren’t just gonna sit there and take it. Kind of the cornerstone of all of my belief in markets and how they work is human ingenuity. That’s what ends up bailing us out. When bad things happen, you don’t just sit there and take it in life — you figure out how to get back on track. I go, so here we have the pandemic that’s hit — that’s a big smash in the mouth to these firms. They’re not just gonna sit there and take it. They’ll figure out how to get back on track. They’ll try something new and different, and along the way there’ll be winners and losers, and I dunno who the winners will be and the losers. what I do believe is that effort, that human ingenuity, will likely get us back on track faster than most people think. BARRY RITHOLTZ : We saw that during the financial crisis. The pandemic was less than a quarter — down 34% from that end of the first quarter in 2020, the S&P was up 69% for the rest of the year. that’s what we’re getting at. I mean, what was going on — and this is what I get back to: what do you tell people to get through the tough times? Go back to first principles. Okay, we have the pandemic, and there were all kinds of forecasts, but the consensus, I remember at the time, was it’s likely to be a two- or three-year kind of phenomenon. the market’s down about 20 or 30%. That seems about right to me. I mean, I don’t know. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So in other words, it’s already in the price, and trying to act in response to something everybody knows seems like a waste of time. I learned that really in the late nineties. I was on an investment committee — I used to sit on investment committees; I don’t anymore, other than our own. the chairman of that investment committee went around the world. This was 1998 — I dunno if you remember — BARRY RITHOLTZ : Sure — Long-Term Capital Management. I was on a trading desk. you had the Russian default, you had the Asian contagion. He goes around the world — the chairman of the committee — and eventually talks about all the problems around the world, and he concludes: so why should we invest in stocks at all? I said, well, you know, I think you’ve characterized what was going on in these different countries. I think all you’ve done is explain why the market’s down 35%. he goes, ah — and we stayed invested, and of course we were amply rewarded. if people could just go through first principles — and by that I mean: bad news comes into the market, they look and they say, aha, the stock is down, now I want to get out ’cause I’m stressed. If we can get them to change their opinion and say, look, the market’s down — I mean, the price is down quite a bit — and that’s probably about right, given the bad news that we have, then: therefore, I need to stay invested. I was thinking the other day, if I come out with a second book, maybe I’ll call it Stay Invested. we’d have Stay Calm and Stay Invested. BARRY RITHOLTZ : I think your second book should be named What Would Gene Fama Say? DAVID BOOTH : There you go. BARRY RITHOLTZ : If the market’s down 30%, what would Fama say? He’d say, it’s in the price. just sit there and relax and stay calm. DAVID BOOTH : And that’s the science, you know. BARRY RITHOLTZ : That’s really interesting. you mentioned some forecasts and predictions. Another aspect of the book is: plan, don’t predict. You can’t foresee the future, so making decisions based on predictions — you’re essentially engaging in wishful thinking. DAVID BOOTH : Well, that’s right. I mean, you need to have a plan for going forward in life and investing, but don’t waste the time on trying to predict the unpredictable. Markets are unpredictable — that’s why the pros can’t beat the market, ’cause markets are unpredictable. over the long haul — if you go back, we haven’t talked about the history, but a hundred years of returns that covers the Great Depression, World War II, the Korean War, high inflation, the Great Financial Crisis, the pandemic — through all of that, 10% a year. I think a lot of what I do now, particularly talking to students, is talk about the miracle of the stock and bond markets. These public markets are truly miracles. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Really, really fascinating. Here’s another thesis that I think is really very, very insightful: control what you can, manage what you can’t. You can’t control crashes, recessions, interest rates, or any of that century of terrible events — but you can manage yourself, your allocation, your ongoing saving. Discuss that a little bit. In terms of dealing with it — it’s all about managing uncertainty. control what you can, and manage what you can’t — manage the uncertain part as best you can. Hey, you can’t eliminate it, but you can manage it. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And by managing it, you’re talking about having a financial plan and sticking to it, continuing to dollar-cost average into it. You can’t control what the Fed does, or what’s happening in the Straits, or who moves. A lot of people, they make portfolio decisions based on their forecast of what the market’s gonna do. That’s a waste of time. You wanna pay attention to what’s going on, because over your lifetime there are gonna be situations when you need to change your investment policy around — but it’s not based on what’s going on in the market. You need to change — you know, you get a new job, you wanna retire, you have a family. You can control how much risk you take, basically. There are two basic decisions as you go down the path. First is the split: how much do you have in stocks at all, versus relatively riskless assets like a money market fund or a bond. you get that right. then the second part is, to the extent you’re investing in stocks, buy the whole market. That makes you as good as the insiders — people that think of themselves as outsiders. That’s another miracle of markets: right now you have it, unlike my parents, who never had that available to ’em. The market is good for everyone. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So let’s talk a little bit about financial media, which you write extensively about in the book. I tell people, look — do you think you have more anxiety today, or people have more anxiety today, than during the Great Depression, or during, say, World War II, when it looked like we were losing at first? Those were real, serious anxieties. I’m not making light of the anxiety, but what the hundred years of data shows us is the market does a really good job of pricing all that uncertainty and the risks. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So another quote in the same section: “In investing, success often comes not from doing more, but from tuning out more.” So I have to share this with you, ’cause every time I write “tune out the noise,” I get a ton of pushback. DAVID BOOTH : Well, first, I’m glad to see you get your share of that — just like I do. DAVID BOOTH : That’s an example of — you go back and reread it, and I’m like, I wrote that? BARRY RITHOLTZ : No, that’s damn fine. it’s because you are implying, hey, this is about securing your family’s future — but it’s not just about money, it’s about all the things that really matter. DAVID BOOTH : And now, coming out this summer and into the fall, we are innovating even more. Right now, we have mutual funds and ETFs that do the same thing — two pools of money doing the same thing. The SEC has given us approval to merge those two, so it’ll just be one pool of assets with two ways of accessing it. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Two different wrappers, same pool of money. DAVID BOOTH : Same pool of money. that will take away the argument — you don’t have to worry about it anymore. BARRY RITHOLTZ : That’s really good. DAVID BOOTH : That actually speaks to how science is developing. It’s not like we sit on our hands — we’re continually trying to work through things and become more efficient. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So let’s talk about another philosophical belief from you guys that I’m fascinated by. People have had a hard time wrapping their heads around: is DFA an indexer? Are they an alpha chaser? the way I kind of explained it to myself was: no — when you look at traditional indexers, they’re just using one factor of the many Fama-French factors, and what Dimensional has said is, hey, we’re going to use three, four, five factors. we are indexers, plus the next four factors on the list. Is that a fair philosophical breakdown? DAVID BOOTH : Yeah, that’s part of what we do — exactly that. there are some people that don’t want to have a bias towards value or small cap, and for those we have kind of plain vanilla funds too, that aren’t biased. in both cases, it’s about execution. We talked about how an index fund has to trade in a bizarre sort of way — and we don’t do that. We apply that thinking to all the funds. that, here again, what we’re trying to do is apply the science, and by the way we structure portfolios, we think we can do better than index providers. then secondarily, the way we trade, relative to the way index funds trade — that’s true in everything we do. then, some clients like to have a small cap bias, some don’t. It’s their money — we try to come up with whatever they think is sensible. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So let’s talk a little bit about philanthropy, ’cause I know part of the book discusses legacy, and you’ve been very involved philanthropically. A decade ago you signed the Giving Pledge, and — I go back two decades — right around the time of the financial crisis, you made a gift in ’08 to the University of Chicago’s business school, which I think was the largest gift ever in the country, or to Chicago, at that time: $300 million. now it’s the Chicago Booth School of Business. Tell us a little bit about what motivated a gift of that size to that recipient, and what are your thoughts 20 years later? DAVID BOOTH : Well, okay, first lemme just say it was kind of funny. The announcement for that was made in November of 2008 — like, the week after Obama got elected for the first time. there was a big announcement at the school — they said, big announcement coming tonight, free food, come on in — and they thought it had something to do with Obama. that’s when they announced that the school’s name was changing. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Which, by the way, wasn’t a requirement of your gift. DAVID BOOTH : Well, I didn’t argue against the Obama part. BARRY RITHOLTZ : I heard through several people that you pushed back initially. DAVID BOOTH : Well, I pushed back a little bit, but not a lot. What happened was, I approached the dean of the business school and said, you know, it’s time for payback here — for what the university has done for me, and the faculty. not only training me in school, but then following up over the years — over the now decades, 45 years. You know, we’ve had five Nobel laureates work very closely with us; all of ’em have been significant directors of our mutual funds or the company, Fama being a founder as well. It’s time for me to pay back, and it’s gotta be a big chunk of what I have. this is what I’m willing to do. the dean looks at it and goes, you know, we were thinking about naming the school, and we weren’t asking for nearly this much — we’ll name the school after you. I go, okay, well, whatever. it was about me wanting to feel good about me. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Well, you feel a sense of obligation to the University of Chicago ’cause of everything they gave you. Undergraduate and pre-PhD, MBA — you were at Kansas, and you gave them a similar number last year: $300 million to the University of Kansas athletics program. Why focus on sports there? What’s so significant about Kansas athletics? ‘Cause, by the way, as a school, they’ve been doing pretty good. DAVID BOOTH : Oh yeah, yeah. Well, first off, Lawrence, Kansas, where the University of Kansas is, is my hometown. I went to Lawrence High School and then the University of Kansas. with all the relatives, it’s in my blood. for a big state school like that, what’s really important is to have a great, competitive athletic program. I mean, I know the arguments — some people go, you know, they’re not so sure about that — BARRY RITHOLTZ : It doesn’t hurt their marketing, their ability to recruit professors, students. It makes the town better. I mean, it just multiplies across everything, regardless of how you feel about big football in college. I happen to love it, and I particularly love college basketball. Kansas has always been really good at basketball, and it’s getting better in football. then with NIL — a little dollop of NIL coming down the pike — BARRY RITHOLTZ : Name, image, likeness. Get some money to the students. DAVID BOOTH : To the students. it puts great financial pressure on the schools, and it’s difficult for a state school to have a big budget for athletics when their professors are making what they’re making. it’s important for private money — for alums and whatever — to step up in order to help them be successful. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And I’m gonna assume that this isn’t the end of your academic gifts — you’re gonna be doing other stuff in the future, and obviously the Giving Pledge is a part of that. I have to ask about a purchase you made in 2010, which is: you bought Naismith’s original document of, essentially, here are the rules of basketball — this is where basketball was invented. I think you paid over $4 million for it, and then you gave it to the University of Kansas athletic department. Explain — tell us about that. DAVID BOOTH : Well, it was really kind of an interesting auction. James Naismith invented basketball in 1891 — if you think about it — BARRY RITHOLTZ : The peach crate. DAVID BOOTH : Yeah, the whole thing. It’s the only major sport that I can think of where we know who invented it. It was a class assignment for him in school, at the YMCA in Springfield, Massachusetts. the rules stayed in the family, and as things happen over time, they just decided that they wanted to sell it. I decided — here again, basketball is so important; if you live in Lawrence, Kansas, you realize that the rules of basketball, those two typewritten pages, need to be in Lawrence, Kansas. ‘Cause Naismith, after he invented the game, goes to teach at Kansas for 40 years; he’s buried in Lawrence. I realized that — BARRY RITHOLTZ : Perfect match. DAVID BOOTH : Match — had to buy it. it started off, they thought it would go for about $2 million, but along the way — I was bidding over the phone, and there was somebody else bidding over the phone, and it kept ratcheting up, and I ended up paying about four and a half million. The person on the other end of the phone was David Rubenstein. DAVID BOOTH : Your Bloomberg — BARRY RITHOLTZ : Co-host — fellow host. Did you explain eventually to him why you bought it and why it went to Kansas? DAVID BOOTH : No — once I paid for it, it was announced who bought it. he sent me an email the next day saying, hey, I think I cost you some money. we still have a good chuckle about that. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So, the last piece of philanthropy I have to ask about before we get to our favorite questions: you’re known as an avid art collector. If you go down — I don’t know what river that is in Texas, but I’ve been on that boat — you can see some of your sculptures right from the river, if you’re in a boat. You’ve endowed a conservation center at the Museum of Modern Art, and — as opposed to just donating a sculpture or a painting — you’re essentially helping them preserve their entire collection in perpetuity. DAVID BOOTH : Well, I mean, preserving your patrimony is important for any country, and art is such a big deal, and MoMA is such a great museum — BARRY RITHOLTZ : Spectacular collection. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Of which, like, 3% is displayed at any time. It’s an enormous, enormous collection. DAVID BOOTH : It’s complicated. I’ve sat on the board there for about 10 years now, and it’s just really been tremendously exciting. then I endowed the conservation lab, because conservation is easy to overlook. taking care of, particularly, modern art — which could be some fiberglass or something — who knows what kind of stuff goes into it — BARRY RITHOLTZ : To say nothing about how paint decays, how canvas, paper — all that stuff is problematic over time. DAVID BOOTH : In the old days, conservation was probably somebody kind of having a couple sips of alcohol and dabbing some paint on a painting and trying to clean it, or whatever. Now it’s incredibly sophisticated — you take X-rays of the painting or whatnot, you study the chemistry of it. I’ve headed up that conservation committee for quite a while now. It’s very exciting to see what they’ve done to maintain the art. All right — I only have you for a couple more minutes, and you and I can continue this conversation in Southern California, in Huntington Beach, in a few weeks. For now, let’s jump to our favorite questions that we ask all of our guests, starting with: tell us about the mentors who helped shape your career. I have a pretty good idea who they are. Let’s just start with the Nobel laureates: Merton Miller and Gene Fama, Myron Scholes, Bob Merton and Doug Diamond. Kind of an impressive group of characters. BARRY RITHOLTZ : That’s a Murderers’ Row right there. DAVID BOOTH : Murderers’ Row, yeah. Then you had Mac McQuown, who really started indexing — BARRY RITHOLTZ : And he really was the initial — was he the first check into DFA? DAVID BOOTH : No, he was a founder. more importantly — besides investing in the funds, he helped us raise the money, the risk capital, for the firm. then I always have to throw in my parents. I mean, it ties into what True Wealth was about. They never had much money, but they were wealthy — they had figured out what life was about. Let’s talk about books, in addition to yours. What are some of your favorites? What are you reading currently? DAVID BOOTH : Well, I just finished 1929, Andrew Ross Sorkin’s new book. BARRY RITHOLTZ : That is on my nightstand — it’s up in a few books in my queue. DAVID BOOTH : Then, in the last couple years, the book I’ve really liked a lot was Paris 1919 by Margaret MacMillan. she takes us through what became known as the Treaty of Paris. When the Armistice was signed at the end of World War I — that’s just when all kinds of crazy things happened, because the Ottoman Empire collapsed, the Russian Empire collapsed, the Austro-Hungarian Empire collapsed. you had to create new countries all over the place — all through Central Europe and the Middle East. It took about six months to develop the Treaty of Paris. The first five or so, they didn’t do much, and then all of a sudden, the last month, they just got together. I don’t know if they could have done much better, but it was pretty chaotic. I’m gonna add that to my list. Tell us — are you streaming anything? What do you do to relax? Podcasts, movies — what entertains you? DAVID BOOTH : Well, I mean, your podcast. — no, we have a new season of Ted Lasso, which I’m really all over. BARRY RITHOLTZ : My wife and I are waiting for there to be more than three or four in the queue. It’s just too frustrating to watch one a week. DAVID BOOTH : By the way, he’s a KU alum as well. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Yes, yes — I knew that. DAVID BOOTH : And we have any number of series. You know, what happened was, when the pandemic hit and we couldn’t go out much, I watched more TV in that two-year period than I ever watched before — or since. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Same — absolutely the same. I was mentioning the other day that 6:30 is the new 7:30. It used to be, if you tried to make a dinner reservation around 7 or 7:30, it was the toughest reservation to get. now it seems the hard reservation to get is 6 or 6:30. it’s not just that we’re aging and heading towards the early bird special.

items.title: 10 Tuesday AM Reads
items.summary: Kick the month off right with your morning reads: • Higher Yields Are a Boon for Muni Bond Buyers: The rise in bond yields has been a good news/bad news story. Treasury, the increase has been disquieting and has elicited an extraordinary scheme to double its buying of long-term maturities to boost their prices and suppress their yields. Hilltop’s Tom Kozlik on municipal yields hitting some of their most compelling levels in years — and unlike Treasuries, munis still reward investors for extending maturities. • How Much Is the Iran War Costing Americans?: John Cassidy on why a proper calculation must take in much more than just the military costs. (New Yorker) see also How the War in Iran Is Redrawing the Global Energy Map: Coco Liu on what six months of disrupted Middle Eastern production and a contested Strait of Hormuz have done — chiefly, pushing governments and consumers toward renewables. • ‘A Roth IRA on Steroids’: Wealthy Americans Find Another Tax-Free Way to Invest: On the tax-free vehicle one adviser calls “a Roth IRA on steroids for people who can afford it and want to leave it to their heirs.” Private-placement life insurance contracts allow unlimited investments to grow tax-free. • America’s Next Grocery Shock Is Brewing: Erica Pandey on the forces piling up beyond beef, coffee, and chocolate — expensive grain, soaring fertilizer, and more. • Scott Bessent Takes On Bond Vigilantes in $32tn Treasury Market: George Steer on the Treasury’s plan, which stunned Wall Street, to “at least double” its purchases of long-term government bonds — dismissed by investors as a “band-aid on a bullet hole” amid a $40tn debt burden and smouldering inflation. (Financial Times) see also What Is Scott Bessent Doing With the $32tn Treasury Market — and Will It Work?: Claire Jones on the former financier’s sternest test yet. • The Online Shopping Trend Where You Buy Nothing: Itika Sharma Punit on South Korea’s “dopamine sites,” where the pleasure comes from browsing, curating, and tracking — not from a delivery. • How Paris swapped cars for bikes – and transformed its streets: Under Anne Hidalgo – mayor for 12 years until last week – the French capital added bike lanes, cut traffic and reclaimed public space, but not without resistance (The Guardian) • These Generals Fought for Israel. Now They See ‘Jewish Terrorism’ as the Threat.: Ronen Bergman on the growing number of former Israeli generals, intelligence officials, and prime ministers accusing West Bank settlers of ethnic cleansing with government support. “Once a society behaves this way, that society is doomed.” (New York Times) • Your Brain May Not Actually “Make” Decisions: Indiana University’s Tom James on why the perceive-then-decide sequence we all imagine may be very different from what actually happens inside the brain. • How Arena Club and Fanatics Are Turning Baseball Cards Into Online Casinos: Derek Jeter, fresh off his Hall of Fame induction, became the face of a startup that digitizes pack-ripping — turning an age-old hobby into something that resembles online gambling. Video of the day: I Tracked Down the Company Ruining Fruit Be sure to check out our Masters in Business with David Booth, Founder, Chairman, and former CEO of Dimensional Funds Advisors. DFA just crossed $1 trillion dollars, and has become the largest active equity ETF manager.

items.title: Uncounted heat-related deaths
items.summary: The U.S Centers for Disease Control and Prevention count causes of death, and heat is included in the tabulations. it is likely that the reports for heat are undercounts. NPR, in collaboration with researchers at Boston University, modeled mortality due to heat and estimate the true counts are five times higher than reported.

items.title: "Colonel Tom Parker" == Andreas Conelis van Kuijk
items.summary: "Colonel Tom Parker" == Andreas Conelis van Kuijk Dolly Parton's passing inspired Josh Marshall to dive deeper into one of the adjacent "Mysteries of Americana", namely how Andreas Cornelis van Kuijk "hopped off a ship in New York City" at the age of 20, in 1929, and eventually managed to set himself up as Elvis Presley's manager Colonel Tom Parker, a "cigar-chomping, hard-charging good ole boy, someone out of central casting or perhaps a comic book", allegedly born in West Virginia rather than in Breda. Marshall's focus is linguistic: "How is it that Parker, a quite prominent public figure for decades, managed to maintain his false identity as well as the fact that he was in the country illegally and pull off his Southern good ole boy persona? He had a Dutch accent, albeit a relatively mild one. [H]ow did Parker pull this off? I had to figure this out. over the weekend I chased this mystery down a true rabbit hole. The answer, to me at least, was as fascinating as the mystery. He kind of didn’t hide it. He had a reasonably good accent. what he did have was affect and he got people to think that he had a bit of a lisp or speech impediment. This also seem to be the reason he came with a fraudulent backstory about being born in West Virginia, despite the fact that his professional life was all around Mississippi and Louisiana and Tennessee.

items.title: How Phone Addiction Keeps You from Achieving a Productive “Flow State”
items.summary: If you have an iPhone, try pushing its side button three times in a row. Just like magic, the screen should turn from color into black-and-white, or rather grayscale. (To do the same on an Android phone, you’ll have to dive into settings, then “accessibility,” “vision enhancements,” and “color correction.”) Why would you want that in the first place? As Harvard Kennedy School and Harvard Business School professor Arthur C. Brooks explains in the Big Think video above, “one of the ways that you can actually get less hooked by social media, or any screen-based technology, is by turning off the color.” When you get only black, white, and the shades of gray in between, “you will care less about your screen, and you will look at it less.” This may ring true to those of us who remember purely monochromatic cellphones, and how little time we spent staring at them. no matter your generation, Brooks has plenty of useful advice about how to break the dependency on your phone from which, as a twenty-first-century internet user, you almost certainly suffer. “You notice when somebody is addicted to heroin, because it’s not that common for ordinary people,” he says. “You don’t notice when somebody’s addicted to their phone, because literally everybody is addicted to their phones.” Therefore, we could all benefit from turning off notifications, setting defined “tech times,” exercising without our devices, and going on multi-day meditation retreats — though we may have to work up to that last one. The functional phone addict may believe that all his daily scrolling may not have that much of a negative impact on his life, and even that it helps him unwind. What he doesn’t realize, in Brooks’ view, is the extent to which digital distractions keep him out of what psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi called “flow.” (These comments come around the 27:06 mark.) Flow happens “when you’re involved immersively in something, and hours turn to minutes. You lose track of time. It’s intensely pleasurable,” almost “like a state of Buddhist meditation.” Consciously or unconsciously, we use our phones and other digital devices in a way that prevents flow, “multitasking” between numerous tasks and distractions, never paying sustained attention to any one thing. At the root of this impulse is a fear of boredom, which must be endured in order to accomplish anything meaningful. The irony of our newfound ability to evade boredom every moment is that, if we do so, the whole of life turns out to be pretty boring.

items.title: Milton Glaser’s 10 Rules for Life & Work: The Celebrated Designer Dispenses Wisdom Gained Over His Long Life & Career
items.summary: “None of us has really the ability to understand our path until it’s over,” the celebrated graphic designer Milton Glaser mused less than a minute into the above video. The late Milton Glaser’s many contributions to pop culture—the I ❤ NY logo, the psychedelic portrait of a rainbow-haired Bob Dylan, DC Comics’ classic bullet logo—conferred undeniable authority. To the outside eye, he seemed to have a pretty firm handle on the path he traveled for lo those many decades. Aspirant designers would do well to give extra consideration to any advice he might have shared. As would the rest of us. His “Ten Things I Have Learned,” originally delivered as part of a talk to the AIGA—a venerable membership organization for design professionals—qualifies as solid life advice of general interest. Yes, the Internet spawns bullet-pointed tips for better living the way spring rains yield mushrooms, but Glaser, a self-described “child of modernism,” did not truck in pithy Instagram-friendly aphorisms. Instead, his list was born of reflection on the various turns of a long and mostly satisfying creative career. We’ve excerpted some of his most essential points below, and suggest that those readers who are still in training give special emphasis to number seven. Don’t place too much weight on number nine until you’ve established a solid work ethic. (See number four for more on that.) MILTON GLASER”S TEN RULES FOR WORK AND LIFE (& A BONUS JOKE ABOUT A RABBIT). YOU CAN ONLY WORK FOR PEOPLE THAT YOU LIKE Some years ago I realized that… all the work I had done that was meaningful and significant came out of an affectionate relationship with a client. IF YOU HAVE A CHOICE NEVER HAVE A JOB Here, Glaser quotes composer John Cage: Never have a job, because if you have a job someday someone will take it away from you and then you will be unprepared for your old age. SOME PEOPLE ARE TOXIC AVOID THEM. Glaser recommends putting a questionable companion to a gestalt therapy test. If, after spending time with that person “you are more tired, then you have been poisoned. If you have more energy, you have been nourished. The test is almost infallible and I suggest that you use it for the rest of your life.” PROFESSIONALISM IS NOT ENOUGH (or THE GOOD IS THE ENEMY OF THE GREAT) Glaser concedes that a record of dependable excellence is something to look for in a brain surgeon or auto mechanic, but for those in the arts, “continuous transgression” is the quality to cultivate. Professionalism does not allow for that because transgression has to encompass the possibility of failure and if you are professional your instinct is not to fail, it is to repeat success. LESS IS NOT NECESSARILY MORE I have an alternative to the proposition that I believe is more appropriate. ‘Just enough is more.’ STYLE IS NOT TO BE TRUSTED Style change is usually linked to economic factors, as all of you know who have read Marx. fatigue occurs when people see too much of the same thing too often. HOW YOU LIVE CHANGES YOUR BRAIN The brain is the most responsive organ of the body…. Thought changes our life and our behavior. I also believe that drawing works in the same way…. Drawing also makes you attentive. It makes you pay attention to what you are looking at, which is not so easy. DOUBT IS BETTER THAN CERTAINTY One of the signs of a damaged ego is absolute certainty. Schools encourage the idea of not compromising and defending your work at all costs. Well, the issue at work is usually all about the nature of compromise…. Ideally, making everyone win through acts of accommodation is desirable. Glaser credits essayist Roger Rosenblatt’s Rules for Aging (misidentifying the title as Aging Gracefully) with helping him articulate his philosophy here. It doesn’t matter what you think. It does not matter if you are late or early, if you are here or there, if you said it or didn’t say it, if you are clever or if you were stupid. If you were having a bad hair day or a no hair day or if your boss looks at you cockeyed or your boyfriend or girlfriend looks at you cockeyed, if you are cockeyed. If you don’t get that promotion or prize or house or if you do – it doesn’t matter. It’s interesting to observe that in the new AIGA’s code of ethics there is a significant amount of useful information about appropriate behavior towards clients and other designers, but not a word about a designer’s relationship to the public. If we were licensed, telling the truth might become more central to what we do. A butcher was opening his market one morning and as he did a rabbit popped his head through the door. The butcher was surprised when the rabbit inquired ‘Got any cabbage?’ The butcher said ‘This is a meat market – we sell meat, not vegetables.’ The rabbit hopped off.

items.title: More nothing now
items.summary: Our kids were playing Settlers of Catan over the holidays. They’d rearranged the strategy game’s hexagonal tiles into an archipelago of islands that no rulebook recognises, imagined ‘bridges’ built from wood, brick and stone, and invented a purpose for the game about network connectivity that had nothing to do with earning points. They were not playing Catan. They were playing in Catan, using its materials as components to make a world the designers never imagined. My first instinct was to reach for the rulebook and teach them how the game actually works. My next was to figure out how I could win. It took me a while to realise what I really needed to do: build up the courage to ask if I could sit in and build with them. That was the moment something shifted – not for the kids, who were already there, but for me: a 48-year-old professor sitting on the carpet, making islands and building bridges without a point in sight. You can play a game or you can play in a game. When you follow the official rules, pursue the stated objective, and measure yourself against opponents or a scoring system, that’s competition: playing a game. The Greeks had a word for this kind of play: agôn, from the god who personified conflict, struggle and contest. when my kids disassembled the board and turned it into a world, they were doing something older and stranger. They were engaged in what the French sociologist Roger Caillois, in his taxonomy Man, Play and Games (1958), called paidia: free, spontaneous, unstructured play. The kind with no winner, no score, and no optimisation. The kind of play that has almost no place in adult life and, arguably, the kind we need the most, especially now, when even our leisure comes with leaderboards. The entire architecture of digital life – with its algorithmic feeds, frictionless production and the ambient expectation that we should be consuming or optimising at all times – nudges us towards chasing outputs rather than generating meaning. We track our sleep and score our calm. Fitness apps turn the morning run into a contest; meditation apps gamify stillness with streak counters; language apps award achievement badges for what used to be called curiosity. Even journaling apps nudge users toward consistency scores. The gamification of leisure has turned into work everything that used to exist as its counterpoint. Leisure has become a third shift with its own metrics, its own guilt, and its own sense of falling behind. The philosopher C Thi Nguyen calls this ‘value capture’: the process by which a game’s simplified, legible values start to colonise the real-world activity the game was supposed to serve. Their power arises from the fact that games don’t just create worlds, but new visions of the good, telling players what to care about by virtue of what the game rewards through scores. When you’re doing Duolingo to maintain your streak, or when your place on the running app’s leaderboard replaces the reason you started running, that’s value capture. The metric ate the meaning. The Dutch historian and cultural critic Johan Huizinga saw this coming almost a century ago. In Homo Ludens (1938), he argued that play is not marginal to civilisation but, rather, generative of it. For Huizinga, law, philosophy, poetry and war all emerge from play’s ‘magic circle’: the bounded space where ordinary rules are suspended and something else becomes possible. Huizinga worried that the play element had been declining in Western civilisation since the end of the 18th century, eroded by industrialisation and professionalisation. What he feared has now been fulfilled. It’s not that we killed play; we captured it and harnessed it to a productivity framework. Then we packaged and sold it for passive consumption. The magic circle was instrumentalised into a dopamine hit. What’s missing is neither ‘fun’ nor ‘competition’. We have plenty of those and, to be clear, I’m a huge fan of both. I grew up playing soccer and skiing. In my teens and 20s, I was a serious rock climber. Later I evolved into a competitive ultramarathon runner and now have 50-plus races under my belt, thousands of miles on trails in my legs, and two age-group national titles to my name. Agôn is what I do on weekends. it’s not where I find meaning, build community, or figure out who I am. A large part of the trouble is that we’ve eliminated the conditions in which free play arises. Watch the subway car on any morning commute. Every head is bowed to a screen. Not working, not thinking, just filling the time. Candy Crush in the checkout line. Instagram between floors in the elevator. Mere seconds of unstructured time trigger panic, and our fingers reach unconsciously for our phones. boredom isn’t a problem; rather, it’s the condition in which the mind, left alone, begins to play by itself, to wander, associate, drift toward the transitional space where unexpected connections assemble unbidden. Every moment that we fill with a screen forecloses the free play of the mind. We don’t just need different games. Caillois saw the full spectrum of play: from agôn (competition) and alea (chance), to mimicry (role-playing) and ilinx (vertigo and disorientation). All four types sit on a continuum between paidia (complete improvisation) and ludus (structured rules). contemporary game culture tends to collapse this entire spectrum into one narrow band: competition plus structure. We have no category (not in the App Store and not in our cultural vocabulary) for paidia without agôn: our culture has no home for free, exploratory, contemplative play that refuses to compete. paidia still erupts wherever people stop keeping score: kids on a playground invent rules then abandon them mid-sentence, Minecraft’s creative mode hosts millions of players building dreamworlds for the sake of building; Lego, at its best, is a pure paidia portal – recombinatory, autotelic, improvisational. these exceptions clarify the problem: Minecraft (owned by Microsoft) and Lego are corporately branded IP ecosystems framed as toys for children. It’s not that free play has vanished, it just exists under constant threat of value capture. We do it in spite of our platforms, not because of them. the kinds of play that refuse to compete or optimise, or produce a measurable outcome, lack cultural prestige and social infrastructure. The British psychoanalyst and paediatrician Donald W Winnicott would have recognised this absence as a clinical emergency. In Playing and Reality (1971), Winnicott argued that play is not what children do on the way to becoming productive adults; it is a crucial part of how human beings maintain their worlds. Through play we become present to our own experience, capable of surprise, alive to the difference between going through the motions and actually being there. Winnicott’s key concept is transitional space, though ‘space’ is misleading here because he has in mind not a location but a condition. Think of a conversation so engrossing that you forget you’re speaking and say something you didn’t know you thought until you heard it leave your mouth. You’re not entirely inside your own head (fantasy) and you’re not entirely performing for an audience (compliance). That in-between zone – neither fully private nor fully public, neither pure inner life nor pure external task – is what Winnicott called transitional space. It’s where creativity, art and what he called ‘imaginative living’ originate. His most radical claim still hits like an urgent diagnosis: ‘It is creative apperception more than anything else that makes the individual feel that life is worth living.’ He contrasts this with compliance, a relationship to external reality that ‘carries with it a sense of futility’. It is worth pausing to unpack this fully. Winnicott is arguing that what makes life meaningful is ultimately not achieving goals, having a family or even making art. It’s about how we see the world. ‘Apperception’ names a mode of encounter in which perception is not passive reception but active engagement. The difference is subtle but decisive: in ordinary perception, the world is simply there and the self adjusts to it; in creative apperception, we co-create the world, forging something between self and environment in the zone of play. Compliance, by contrast, is life lived on someone else’s terms, following scripts, bowing before scores and metrics: moving through a world already defined in advance. Nothing new is risked, nothing genuinely one’s own is made. Most people, Winnicott believed, experience just enough creativity to recognise its absence, sensing that they are mostly ‘living uncreatively, as if caught up in the creativity of someone else, or of a machine.’ That last sentence, written in 1971, strikes me as the most prescient insight from 20th-century psychology for our time. Long before the personal computer, before the algorithm, and before we voluntarily installed surveillance engines in our pockets and called them phones, Winnicott worried about being caught up in the creativity of a machine. He also had a solution: play. For Winnicott, play is the condition of feeling real on a daily basis. Friedrich Schiller, writing almost two centuries before Winnicott, made the same case from the other direction. In On the Aesthetic Education of Man (1795), he argued that human beings are torn between the pull of raw sensation and the push toward abstract order, and that only what he called the ‘play drive’ integrates both. Schiller wrote that ‘man only plays when he is in the fullest sense of the word a human being, and he is only fully a human being when he plays.’ Winnicott tells you what play does psychologically: it makes life feel real. Schiller tells you what it does metaphysically: it makes you whole. Simply put: adults need play as desperately as children do – a zone where inner life meets outer materiality and something unpredictable emerges. The Greeks, of course, had a term for this. Aristotle’s medieval fanboy Thomas Aquinas identified eutrapelia, the habit of knowing when and how to play well, as a genuine and discrete virtue. A person who never plays is as disordered as one who never works. I’m not talking about ‘work-life balance’, an exhausted metaphor that still treats play as recovery time for the next productive thing. To practise the virtue of eutrapelia means that a good life requires play. The question, then, isn’t whether to play. It is where does the practice live, and how can we regain it in our daily lives, and valorise it in our culture. For years, I’ve commuted on foot from Grand Central Station to 14th Street, 30 blocks, give or take. I told myself it was exercise, or that I was saving the subway fare, or that I liked the air. the truth is I was thinking. Or rather, I was letting thinking happen. The lecture I couldn’t outline at my desk would assemble itself somewhere around 34th Street, the important points falling into sequence with my footfalls, the argument clarifying as if the motion itself were doing the editing. I wasn’t working on the lecture. I was walking in it, the way my kids were playing in Catan. Walking increased the capacity to generate multiple solutions to open-ended problems by 60 per cent The experience is ancient and well-documented. Friedrich Nietzsche reputedly walked six to eight hours every day, and insisted in his Twilight of the Idols (1889) that ‘Only thoughts that come by walking have any value.’ Aristotle’s Lyceum was called the peripatetic school for its walkways (peripatoi). Jean-Jacques Rousseau claimed that he could compose only while walking. Albert Einstein walked from his home at Princeton, New Jersey to the Institute for Advanced Study and back each day, and supposedly told colleagues that the walk was where the real thinking happened; the office was where he wrote it down. Contemporary research confirms these intuitions, this idea that walking is a form of play for the mind as well as the feet. In 2014, Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz at Stanford University found that walking increased divergent thinking – the capacity to generate multiple solutions to open-ended problems – by roughly 60 per cent. Curiously, a treadmill facing a blank wall worked nearly as well as wandering Stanford’s campus, suggesting that it’s the exercise, not the scenery, producing the results. Metronomic motion allows the thinking to arrive. Push the body further and something stranger happens. Caillois’s taxonomy includes a category almost nobody talks about: ilinx, the play of vertigo and disorientation. Or running past the point where the split times stop mattering and the self loosens its grip. I know this territory from the inside. The first question at the start of a 100-mile race isn’t whether your legs are ready. It’s whether your mind is: wanting to win might get you to the start-line of your local 5K, but agôn won’t get you to the finish of an ultra-marathon. it’s a love of trails that makes those miles magical. Nguyen would call this striving play. The goal exists to make the experience of striving possible, not the other way around. The finish line is just the means; the journey is the destination. Our son does something similar in our basement, though his materials are metal, wood and stone rather than miles of trail. He crafts with scraps of found steel, fixes electric motors, carves wooden animals, shapes copper into jewellery and stone into rings. No tutorial dictates the sequence. The material teaches the craft: copper tells you what it wants to become; stone suggests a shape and you listen or it breaks. At the workbench, inner vision meets the friction of the physical world and something neither planned nor accidental emerges. Wherever adults build or stumble into transitional space, play is doing its work even if we’re not keeping score My son doesn’t sell what he makes. He gives it away: the knife to a friend, the carved animal to a teacher. Play pursued for its own sake, with no metric and no market, overflows into generosity precisely because nothing was extracted. When something beautiful emerges from a process that asked for nothing, the most natural thing in the world is to give it away. What he makes enters the world not as commodity but as gift. I see the same dynamic at my day job, though, again, the materials are different. I’m a professor of literary studies, and the best sessions in my seminars have nothing to do with instruction. They obey the logic of improv: ‘yes, and’. A student notices something strange in a passage (a word that doesn’t fit, a silence where speech should be) and someone else picks it up, turns it over, connects it to something from three weeks ago, and suddenly the room is thinking a thought nobody walked in with. The seminar, at its best, builds transitional space inside an institution that mostly rewards compliance. It opens up the zone between private thought and public evaluation, where a student says something she didn’t know she believed until she heard it leave her mouth.
