items.summary: • The Debt-Equity Distinction: A Century of Policy by Accident: Daniel Peris asks what if much of what we treat as normal is a historical fluke. Modern finance could not exist without widespread debt financing — and the rules that produced it were never really designed. • The Moose That Roared: Why US will lose its trade war with Canada: Paul Krugman on how quickly the unthinkable arrived. Two years ago a US–Canada trade war would have seemed absurd — same language, soldiers who died alongside ours in Afghanistan, free trade agreements since 1988, the most recent signed by Trump himself. • The $500 Billion Experiment to Build 24/7 Markets on Blockchain: Trade.xyz, a little-known market built on top of crypto exchange Hyperliquid, allows speculators to buy and sell blockchain-based oil derivatives continuously, even when traditional markets are closed. The platform has generated some $500 billion in trading volume since launching in October and accounts for more than 99% of activity across Hyperliquid’s third-party market system. It’s About Time: Julia Angwin argues that one of the most powerful media companies in the world and one of the most valuable members of the S&P 500 is at the start of a long, slow decline — with aftershocks for the economy and for society. (New York Times) see also Meta Is Dying: David Dayen and Matt Stoller take up Angwin’s argument, casting Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp as zombie businesses in the mold of Yahoo, Myspace, and AOL after their peaks. • The Trump Intervention That Got the DOJ Off Live Nation’s Back: The antitrust case set out to force the concert giant to sell Ticketmaster. After two White House meetings, the settlement left the company intact.Antitrust case started out aiming to force concert giant to sell Ticketmaster. After two White House meetings, a deal kept the company intact. • Once banished to trailer parks, manufactured homes are moving to suburbia: Long stigmatized and banned by many towns and cities, factory-built housing is being reconsidered in some places because of soaring home prices. Julie Weil on factory-built housing getting a second look from towns that long banned it outright — a stigma that soaring prices are steadily eroding. • It Is Past Time for You to Quit Elon Musk’s X: The case that whatever value the network still holds no longer covers what staying on it costs you. Yes, I’m talking to you. 🫵 (Public Comment) • Behind the Mysterious Symbols Spray-Painted on Our Streets: Michael Kimmelman on markings you have registered a thousand times without once stopping to read — a cross between hieroglyphics and graffiti tags, telling excavators what lies below before the digging starts. You may have registered but never stopped to think about all those colored markings around the city. The marks are everywhere, hiding in plain sight. A cross between hieroglyphics and graffiti tags, they’re mostly put there to tell excavators what’s below ground before crews start digging up the streets. • Why Scientists Are Using Cheap Picnic Coolers to Protect Some of the World’s Most Endangered Animals: Benji Jones reports from Palau, where a super typhoon had churned the famously postcard-blue water, on low-tech coral rescue in a country with some of the strictest marine protections anywhere. Climate change is killing coral reefs, but this low-tech approach could lessen its destruction. • Hacks Star Kaitlin Olson Laughed and Grieved at the Same Time: While filming her final episode of Hacks, the actor and Emmy nominee was also losing her father, the man who first taught her how to be funny. Video of the day: The Bet Shaq Lost That Made Him $500 Million Richer Be sure to check out our Masters in Business this past weekend with Alex Morris of TSOH Investment Research.

Transcript: Alex Morris, “Buffett and Munger Unscripted
items.summary: The transcript from this week’s, MiB: Alex Morris, “Buffett and Munger Unscripted,” is below. You can stream and download our full conversation, including any podcast extras, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube (video), YouTube (audio), and Bloomberg. All of our earlier podcasts on your favorite pod hosts can be found here. MASTERS IN BUSINESS Alex Morris, Author, Buffett and Munger Unscripted BARRY RITHOLTZ : This weekend on the podcast, another extra special guest. Alex Morris is the author of “Buffett and Munger Unscripted.” The amazing story of how he put this book together: by reading and watching 31 years of annual shareholder meetings — thousands and thousands of questions, hundreds and hundreds of hours of video — distilled into a fairly digestible compendium. I thought the book was fascinating and the conversation was fascinating, and I think you will too. With no further ado, my interview of Alex Morris. BARRY RITHOLTZ : I’m Barry Ritholtz. My extra special guest this week is Alex Morris. He is the founder of the TSOH Investment Research Service, launched in 2021 after 10 years as a buy-side equities analyst. He is the author of “Buffett and Munger Unscripted: Three Decades of Investment and Business Insights from the Berkshire Hathaway Annual Shareholder Meetings.” Amazon named it one of the best books of 2025. It’s pretty beefy — I’ve been reading it over the past, I don’t know, eight months. It’s about 500 pages, and I have really, really been enjoying it. I’ve been enjoying it so much that I reached out to Alex and said, let’s talk about your research and the book. He has been a Berkshire Hathaway shareholder since 2011 and attended multiple annual meetings, including the 2026 meeting, the first of the Greg Abel era. Alex Morris, welcome to Bloomberg. ALEX MORRIS : Thank you for having me. As I was saying to you before, Bloomberg headquarters is quite a building. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Nice place to be. ALEX MORRIS : I’m gonna drop my resume on the way out. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So before we get to your resume, let’s roll back to what led you to where you are today. Both a bachelor’s and an MBA from the University of Florida — was finance always the career plan? When I went to school, I really didn’t have any idea what I was gonna do, and my dad’s a plumber, so at first I did building construction, and took a couple physics classes and some other things that kind of threw me for a loop. then I got my first internship working down in Miami, outside all day, and fairly quickly realized, let me find something a little easier. I went to finance. BARRY RITHOLTZ : What were you doing, working outside all day in Miami over the summers? ALEX MORRIS : What were we doing? We were working on a high-rise that was being built, and I spent most of the time running from the rain that came every single day at noon or one o’clock. BARRY RITHOLTZ : I spent a summer in college working with a crew, building decks, swinging a sledge, breaking up the concrete of an old pool to put in a new pool. nothing makes you wanna buckle down and study more than physical labor. It’s like, oh my God, this is really hard work. I have tremendous respect for people who do that. It really forces you to see the world in a different way, doesn’t it? It’s very different work than sitting and writing a book, as you and I both know. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So after you get your bachelor’s and MBA in finance, you take the CFA exam — it’s a two-part exam — and you spend a decade as a buy-side equities analyst. What did you learn from those 10 years on the buy side? ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, a lot. I kept my head down and learned as much as I could every single day. The first job I started at, I was brought in and basically told, hey, you’re running all the research for equities, but also you’re the secretary and you’re doing the trading — you’re doing everything else. I got a lot of good experience there, but it was a role where my boss really was like, just go do what you think makes sense to do, which works really well with my kind of disposition. as time went on, I learned a lot from making a lot of mistakes — that’s a really good way to learn — a ton of reading, a ton of writing online and sharing stuff with people, getting good feedback. yeah, just time and effort. BARRY RITHOLTZ : That’s one of the big problems with everybody: here’s what a billionaire’s morning routine is like. You seem to learn more — all of us learn more from our errors and mistakes than we do from our victories. Do these guys have anything to say about that? ALEX MORRIS : Oh, yeah. They say learn all you can, particularly from other people’s mistakes if you can. that seems to be hard to avoid, at least for me and most of us. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So after 10 years on the buy side, you launch an independent research service in 2021. What made you take that leap? What were those initial couple of years like? ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, I’d been writing online going back to college, and I continued to write online under a pseudonym, Science of Hitting, or TSOH. again, I had built a network over time. I really enjoyed the process of writing. I had started making some supplemental income through writing, and I looked around and I saw people like Ben Thompson of Stratechery and other people who had built a business online sharing their research, I wanna call it that. when I saw Substack come around, and it went from having to understand anything on the technical side to write-in-Word, copy, paste — which is more my speed for technology — I decided to give it a shot. I said, I’ll give myself a year, and if it doesn’t work out, I’ll go find another traditional job, but I wanna see if I can do this. thankfully, it’s worked out. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And “The Science of Hitting” was a book by Ted Williams that Buffett loves to cite for the whole strike zone analogy. If you Google image search this, there’s a strike zone, and Ted Williams literally figured out every position a ball can be thrown — just picture a grid, 12 by, I don’t know, 20, however many it is — and figured out the batting average for when a ball hit that spot, how likely he was to hit it. Why did you name your research service after it? ALEX MORRIS : I’d say partly luck. I don’t know if at the time I knew it was an analogy that I liked so much, and that it would be a good name to keep for the next — you know, coming up on 15 years now. it really spoke to the way I think about investing, in terms of being patient and then also making big swings when you get the chance to. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Waiting for your pitch. when it finally comes, don’t be afraid. I’m gonna assume you’re not averse to a concentrated portfolio. BARRY RITHOLTZ : How many holdings do you typically have at any given time? ALEX MORRIS : In the range of 10 to 15. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Oh, really? big, big swings after waiting for your pitch. there’s names — like you said, I’ve owned Berkshire since 2011, I’ve owned Microsoft since 2011. Most of the positions have been in there for a period of years. you know, it tends to be things that I’ve come to know quite well and have gotten familiar and comfortable with. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So this raises the obvious question: when did you first become enamored of Buffett and Munger, if you’ve been a shareholder since 2011? When did they first show up on your radar? ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, the late 2000s, when I was in school. I stumbled across the letters, and actually a buddy and I both became obsessed with it. We were at the University of Florida, and we actually drove to one of the annual meetings in Omaha. BARRY RITHOLTZ : It’s like a 10-hour drive? ALEX MORRIS : No, it’s like 20 or 25. ALEX MORRIS : It’s a long way. ALEX MORRIS : And we were college kids with no money, right? we slept in the car, I think, one or two nights. ALEX MORRIS : So yeah, we were very interested in it. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Wait, you’re college kids, you have no money — but you didn’t own Berkshire A or B back then? ALEX MORRIS : I think I bought one share — a B share, to be clear. Just to go, for the sake of getting in. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Right, it’s open to anybody who’s a shareholder. What was that first trip as college kids to the Woodstock of Capitalism in Omaha like? ALEX MORRIS : I mean, it’s tough to remember now. I don’t know how productive the trip was, but it was more just being in awe of seeing everything and, you know, really starting to learn about investing. I didn’t do much. Now when I go, I go to a bunch of events and other things and network with people. At that time, it was walking around the convention center eating Dilly Bars, something like that. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So you have sort of the opposite version, the inverse version, of how the sell side or typical newsletters operate. You disclose your buy or sell before you make the trade. You tell your subscribers, this is what I’m planning on doing. Why run it that way? It’s the inverse of the typical way. I think one part of finance that I didn’t love was what I considered a lot of talking about things that weren’t really particularly meaningful. a lot of discussions about things like, “we like Google stock,” for example — but then not a discussion around position sizing, or when you like Google, what are you gonna sell to fund Google? Those kind of more detailed discussions around portfolio management and decision-making. when I launched TSOH, I thought one way to differentiate this is to just take everything away and be completely transparent about all my decisions, my returns, et cetera. I thought there’d be a group of people — maybe not the largest group, but a group of people — who would connect with that, and, you know, I could build a sustainable business as a result. BARRY RITHOLTZ : I recall way back when, watching some talking heads on TV, and when they’d say “we like Google,” or whatever stock it happened to be, the immediate question was, what does that mean? Does that mean you own it? Does that mean you’re holding it? Like, liking a stock is very different than “I have allocated 6% of my portfolio to this position.” BARRY RITHOLTZ : And post-analyst scandal, they used to put the disclosures on screen. We seem to have moved away from that. It’s tough to get on there and kind of explain these things, and a lot of it’s not black or white — it’s in the gray, a lot of these decisions, and there’s a lot of mental accounting and decision-making. I think it’s just a reality of being an individual and being an investor, and it’s figuring out what are you comfortable with and what game are you trying to play. you know, I think talking about that resonates with some people who are kind of honest with themselves about what this game actually is. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So I like the hundred percent transparency and the disclosure prior to trading, but it raises one question. When you are this public, does it make it more difficult to change your mind, or say, hey, we got this wrong and we’re now selling this? ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, and that’s probably fair. It’s never fun to be wrong, of course. It’s less fun to be wrong when you’re telling people that you were wrong and you’re dealing with the pain of that. You know, the way I write my research, I kind of view it as an ongoing discussion for a given name. there’s a lot of opportunities to link back to prior work and go, hey, this call is looking good for X, Y, Z reasons, or looking bad for X, Y, Z reasons. It allows for a continuity of thought and a level of honesty and transparency that I think kind of makes it easier to deal with that issue. BARRY RITHOLTZ : The reason I asked this question was due to a quote right from the book, which is Charlie Munger’s: “Show me the incentive and I will show you the outcome.” First of all, I think that could be the most quoted line of his of all time. how do you contextualize that? Is the whole transparency an attempt to stay honest within the Munger framework? yeah, it’s part of — and it goes back to writing when I was much younger and didn’t know nearly as much as I hopefully do today — it’s part of this just being a continual learning process. it’s with the subscriber, and it’s also me on my own. I think we’re collectively moving to a place where we can become better investors, or at least more thoughtful investors. BARRY RITHOLTZ : I like that concept of becoming a better investor. I don’t remember — the problem with the book is, was that a Buffett quote? Was that a Munger quote? They all kind of blur together. The compounding of knowledge that you’re referring to — I think that’s a Munger observation. ALEX MORRIS : I forget as well. BARRY RITHOLTZ : But one thing that he definitely said was, Warren Buffett got better after 65. “We’re both learning machines, and we spend most of the day reading.” Explain — these guys are running hundreds of billions of dollars, or at least they were, and they spend their day reading. I think it’s all about trying to expand your circle of competence and learning as much as you can. As we said, learning from the mistakes, and the mistakes of others. it’s a game where — you know, I’m thinking, as I’m getting a little bit older, when I go running some time, my knee hurts more and more, while in investing, I’m still quite young, ’cause in theory I could be doing this for another 40, 50 years. all I need to do is be able to sit in a chair, which isn’t that difficult. yeah, as long as you put the time and the effort in and remain open-minded — which is a huge thing that I think especially traditional value investors, Buffett and Munger fans, the last 15 years have been a good lesson in, in terms of being flexible and willing to learn. the world’s obviously changed very significantly. Just turning your mind off from trying to learn about tech, as an example — you can’t really do that anymore in today’s world. You have to be able to at least try to learn about some of these things. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So I know at TSOH you cover a number of individual names — things like Netflix, Microsoft. Ten to 15 names is pretty tight. Tell us about some of your other names, and are you sitting tight with all of these? ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, so as I said before, I’ve owned Microsoft and Berkshire for a long time. I’ve owned Disney for a while, which has not worked out, but thankfully it taught me things about the business that then led to a decent Netflix investment back in ’22. I was curious why you think it didn’t work out. Was it Netflix as a threat, or was it something else? ALEX MORRIS : They saw where the world was going too late, and in their ability to truly pivot and make the investments they needed to make, they were behind. I think they’ve done better than a lot of their peers, at least among the legacy media companies, but they were slow to the party. I think especially with ESPN, they’ve struggled with, what really is our strategy going forward? They have their strategy on the entertainment programming side, but in live programming and sports, it’s still really a challenge of how do we get from A to B over time. obviously sports are expensive. it’s been an issue for them. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And yet, go back a few decades, they were very aggressive. They bought Star Wars, they bought Pixar. Those seemed like — wow, those $4 billion deals, that seems crazy. it’s been a giant moneymaker for them. Was it just a change of leadership at Disney? What led to this failing to recognize the changing world? ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, I think the media companies got lulled into a place where they thought Netflix or these other channels were incremental, as opposed to replacing what they were doing. by the time they figured that out, you know, you’d gotten through a period where Netflix had been investing very aggressively and was going global and getting scale in a way that nobody else has basically been able to catch up to. it changed a lot of their negotiating position amongst each other, and also how they had to price their products, and the reach and engagement of those products. They’re in a really tough place — or have become in a really tough place — relative to Netflix’s rise. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Give us one more holding that is intriguing. One that at one point I would’ve probably thought I’d never own — it speaks to what I said before about reading about a company and writing a company up and following it for a couple years — is Peloton. When they brought Barry McCarthy on as CEO, who used to be at Spotify, that’s where my interest came from. The company went through a transition process — it still continues to this day; he has since left. the stock got to a point where it appeared to be very cheap— ALEX MORRIS : Post-pandemic, yeah. BARRY RITHOLTZ : It had a crazy run-up when everyone was stuck at home and couldn’t get to the gym. Obviously, as did others in that space, but they were the poster child, right? I mean, I think it was a $150 stock at one point, and recently it traded below $4. That’s a 96, 97% drop. ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, it’s pretty amazing. I think there’s this question of, what are they dealing with that’s cyclical versus structural? I think people have a certain view on it that is kind of informed by their anecdotal experience. you look at other industries — like mattresses, for example — where volumes are still meaningfully below what they were during the pandemic. I think most people would argue that’s probably not structural. People still need mattresses, but the supply-demand got outta whack. in Peloton’s case, they went from 500,000 paid customers to 3 million in 36 months. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Paying a monthly subscription fee on top of everything. it’s a little bit of a razor blade model as well. Now they’ve bled off half a million, so they’re at two and a half. you know, if you step back and in the fullness of time went, hey, you guys are gonna go from 500,000 in ’19 to 2.5 million in ’26, everybody would say that’s great. Their strategy got outta line, their cost structure got outta line — I think they’re rectifying that now. again, you’ve got a stock that in my mind was incredibly cheap. it went from something that I probably didn’t think I would’ve ever owned a couple years ago to — it has been my largest position lately. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Oh, interesting. ALEX MORRIS : Another one that I bought recently, or relatively recently, is Dollar Tree. I think it’s a really interesting retail concept that is kind of on its own in the retail landscape. I mean, everybody competes with everybody in retail, but their position, and who they serve, and what they sell to them, is unique. BARRY RITHOLTZ : No threat from the internet at Dollar Tree? BARRY RITHOLTZ : What about from Amazon, or places like that? Or Target, where — you know, I can’t remember the last time I stepped into a Target, but I get Target deliveries every couple of months on a regular basis. It’s so delightful not to have to spend a couple of hours doing that. Dollar Tree sells product at a price point — obviously, it’s very low. The average ticket’s really small. The immediacy of the purchase is a tight window. The ability to cost-effectively do it with delivery is challenging, to say the least. They owned Family Dollar for a long time, which is a Dollar General competitor. They tried to turn it around, and it didn’t work. I was watching from the sidelines for a long time. As they got that resolved, they changed the strategy to basically replicate what a company called Dollarama has already done in Canada. if you look at that, the stock’s been a great performer and the business has done particularly well. I think there’s a lot of sense in the strategic evolution that they’re making, and the stock got pretty cheap — I think I bought in the second half of ’24. yeah, it’s a business — retail, again, obviously is intensely competitive, but there’s little niches that people play in that I think can be attractive, and Dollar Tree is one of those niches. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Really interesting. Coming up, we continue our conversation with Alex Morris, author of “Buffett and Munger Unscripted,” discussing how he plowed through hundreds of hours and 31 years’ worth of material to write this book. You’re listening to Masters in Business on Bloomberg Radio. He is the author of “Buffett and Munger Unscripted: Three Decades of Investment and Business Insights from the Berkshire Hathaway Annual Shareholder Meetings.” So I found the book fascinating, but before we delve into the content, I have to discuss your process. Back in 2018, Berkshire releases the full archive of every Berkshire Hathaway annual meeting from 1994 forward. That’s 31 years’ worth of stuff, and you watch all of it — hundreds of hours, maybe even thousands of hours, 1,700 questions. Where do you begin with an archive that immense? ALEX MORRIS : Yeah — slowly, and somewhat unwillingly at first. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Did you just go back to ’94 and start plowing through? Was there a method to the madness? ALEX MORRIS : Originally — well, first of all, when I was in college and got interested in investing, one of the books that really resonated with me was “The Essays of Warren Buffett,” which Lawrence Cunningham— BARRY RITHOLTZ : I went to grad school with him. ALEX MORRIS : He had the decades of shareholder letters, which you could just sit and plow through if you want, or he compiled it in a way where you could look at, what about capital returns to shareholders? — and look by topic. BARRY RITHOLTZ : He had a much easier task, ’cause the letters are a couple of pages — 10, 20 pages each — and they’re already in print format. You had to fight your way through hundreds and hundreds of hours of video. How did you organize that material? ALEX MORRIS : Well, originally it was only on CNBC’s website, with a web player where you couldn’t speed up the time. one of those where, when you try to fast-forward 20 seconds, it goes 15 minutes and you can’t get back to your original spot. that made it a little bit tough. When it eventually got on YouTube, that helped a ton. I originally went through it for the sake of learning and using it as writing material for TSOH. as time went on — well, first I thought somebody else would do this, so I wouldn’t have to do it. then I didn’t see anybody doing it. At one point, Harriman House reached out to me about writing a book, and I actually was working on something. Basically, the concept was for people like my parents or my grandparents, who had asked me questions about working with a financial advisor or managing their own finances. I was trying to write a book about how do you navigate that relationship with a financial advisor, and talking about active and passive and asset allocation. then I started writing it, and as I got into it, I thought, well, one, I’m not hugely interested in this, and two, I don’t have the depth of knowledge on things like trusts or estates or a lot of financial planning stuff that’s a really important part of that discussion. I just don’t really have the depth of knowledge there — I shouldn’t be the person writing this. when Harriman House reached out, I first said, you know, I have this book, but I think I’m gonna kind of drop it, and I don’t really have anything else. then a week or two later, I wrote back to them and said, I think actually I might have something with the Berkshire meetings that I could explore a little more. I can’t do it unless I reach out to Berkshire and get, if not approval, at least not disapproval from them. BARRY RITHOLTZ : You don’t want them fighting you every step of the way. I put together a sample chapter and sent it to Warren’s assistant at the time, Debbie, and asked, can I please do this? I promised that I’m a massive fan of Warren and Charlie, and I’ll do a good job, and I’ll give away half the proceeds to Glide, which is a charity that Warren supported through the lunch auctions. I got a response a couple days later saying, as long as you’re saying he didn’t approve this, you’re okay to go with it. at that point I was like, okay, now I actually have to do this. the process at first was not particularly well thought out. I remember I got through two or three or four meetings, and I realized I wasn’t getting to a place where I wasn’t gonna have to repeat that process again. I went back to the start, created an Excel file where I timestamped everything, had like primary topic and secondary topic, and then a very simple green, yellow, red: is this gonna be in, or maybe be in? As time went on, I had a lot of overlapping things — I had to figure out which answer was better, which one should I keep. as I got through 10 or 15 years, I knew what I was doing at that point. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Did it reveal itself to you as you were working? By the way, full disclosure: Harriman House is my publisher. one of the things I found fascinating about the writing process is when you happen onto a good framework, it sort of opens itself up to you. It reveals itself, and like, oh, I see what this should look like. I would imagine you might have had a similar experience — year after year, the same themes, the same ideas, although they must evolve over time somewhat. I got to a point where — well, one, yes, the meetings definitely have their place in time, as is kind of revealed — I mean, especially think of like the late nineties, or you get to the financial crisis, the discussions that are had there. The part of it that I found so useful, that I thought would resonate with people, was, you know, the letters are edited, and Warren’s very specific about what he says— BARRY RITHOLTZ : Unscripted is very different. ALEX MORRIS : Unscripted, when they’re off the cuff. Charlie a lot of the time pushes Warren in directions that he may not want to go. The answers would be really revealing. again, in a period like the late nineties, when people were really pressing them on, why aren’t you investing in tech companies — you know, as they’re pushing them, they get a little bit more honest and say things in a slightly different way than if they had written them. anyways, as I worked through it, I just got to a point where I could imagine myself, the college kid, reading this book and getting a lot of value out of it. I also could see myself, the person today who has a lot more experience, reading it and still getting value. I thought, this is gonna be a worthwhile book for a wide range of people, so it hopefully could be a good project. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So a recurring theme of all of the meetings, and therefore of the book: investing success is a temperament problem, not an IQ problem. Emotional stability, patience, and independence from crowd opinion do the compounding. Again, I don’t remember which of them I’m taking the quote from, but we’ve heard that over and over again. Give us a little color on temperament versus IQ. I mean, I think your book title sums it up well — “How Not to Invest.” What mistakes are you looking to avoid is a great place for starting to figure out where you’re trying to go. I think that’s what they’ve done their entire career. it’s funny how that mindset of “don’t be stupid” can still be connected to really big swings at points in time, ’cause that seems like an aggressive act and kind of a risky thing. I think when you actually pair ’em together, they can work well. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So the flip side of the Munger quote “be less stupid” is a Buffett quote: if you have an IQ of 160, well, you can sell 30 points — they’re not needed in investing. That goes and flies against everything we’ve ever heard about, you know, the genius hedge fund manager, the quants, the math whizzes. clearly both Charlie and Warren — not dumb guys, right? They were more than less stupid. how sincere is that — hey, you don’t need 160, and it’s probably gonna get in your way anyway? ALEX MORRIS : I definitely think the latter part is true. It’s very easy to get overconfident in your abilities and to make mistakes that can be — particularly when you start doing things with options or leverage — you can make mistakes that are truly devastating. if you just avoid those things, it’s much easier to, at a minimum, stay in the game. to get to a decent place is also, I don’t think, overly difficult as a starting point. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So over the three decades that the book covers, there have been wildly different environments, where there were those examples of people who should have been less stupid. you had Long-Term Capital Management blow up in — what was that, ’98? — the dot-com implosion, the financial crisis, the zero interest rate policy of the 2010s, then COVID. How do the same principles that are espoused by Buffett and Munger apply to all these wildly different environments? I think it’s being consistently level-headed and not letting things get away from you, and having a long-term view, and staying within your circle — which I think is one of the biggest lessons I’ve had as an investor: learning what game you are playing and why you’re playing that game. your answer may be different from mine. I think a funny example is, someone asked in one of the meetings about Peter Lynch, and Warren Buffett was talking about it and said, his approach works well for him and mine works well for me, and I think if he tried to adopt my approach, it would not work as well — and vice versa. There’s more than one way to get to heaven in this game. as long as you understand that, I think you’re at least at a good starting point. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Another quote that I can’t remember which of them said: volatility is the friend of the investor who knows values, and the enemy of the one who doesn’t. Well, sometimes in real life it feels a little different than that, when you’re seeing a lot of volatility in your portfolio. I think the idea is a sensible one, which is you don’t want your decisions to be led by the market. You want to be making decisions that are somewhat independent of what the market’s telling you. There’s a fine line there between just being stubborn and overconfident — I think especially when you’re younger. A quote like that — and this is true of a lot of quotes from Warren and Charlie — a little bit of experience helps you understand what they’re actually saying, versus maybe a more novice interpretation that can get you in trouble. I think to completely disregard what the market’s saying is something that you should do cautiously, but the idea of acting based on what the facts tell you, as opposed to, you know, the short-term weighing machine, is the right mindset to have in investing. BARRY RITHOLTZ : There are so many quotes of theirs that have just become so famous and repeated over and over again. What sort of buried gems did you find in there that people don’t really talk about? What stands out as, how is this not a more famous line? ALEX MORRIS : I mean, I think some of the discussions on, again, things like stock option accounting in the late nineties, where — I think they say in the book, there were 500 companies, and two of them had adopted, quote-unquote, the right stock option accounting rules. Everybody else was playing this kind of game. they talk about things like that so clearly, in a way that anybody can understand, that it’s just so useful to hear those things. I’m trying to think of other examples throughout the book that stand out. One example they give, in terms of their business, is National Indemnity Insurance Company. They talk about this idea of, there was a period of time where the volumes in that insurance business went up, I believe, five-x, then over a period of 15 years contracted 85%. That’s back below the original starting line. you could imagine running a business and how painful that is. they use it to teach a lesson — it applies differently in different businesses, but how in the insurance business, the only thing that matters is writing good business. you have to get to a place where all the stakeholders, particularly employees, realize that writing bad business is not the decision to make. you have to help them appreciate that they can keep their job, too, as you go through this. it’s just an example of them laying out something that, when they explain it, is so sensible and logical. you have to have that long-term mindset. again, when you compare something like that to how a lot of public companies act, you start to notice things that you may want to avoid. BARRY RITHOLTZ : That’s very much a Science of Hitting philosophy. You’re better off not writing bad business — not writing any business — than writing bad business. I think the modern Berkshire is underappreciated for the importance of the various insurers. there’s GEICO, there’s Berkshire Re, there’s a few insurance companies, which essentially gave Warren a giant pool of capital — and patient capital — to work with. Talk about the significance of insurance to the success of Berkshire Hathaway. ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, it’s been hugely important. That float has — I don’t know what the number is now, but it’s grown very significantly over a long period of time, and it has allowed them to make the investments that have, you know, gotten Berkshire to where it is today. One example that I come back to a lot, from one of those investments, is Coca-Cola. Everybody knows that Berkshire owns Coca-Cola. I think the part that people sometimes don’t know is that Warren started buying in, I believe it was ’88 or ’89, and he bought his last share in ’94. he hasn’t bought or sold a single share since then. At a point in time, it was more than 30% of Berkshire’s equity portfolio — it’s not like it was 2% of their portfolio that they’re not touching. It was a hugely important position, and he hasn’t touched it for more than 30 years. Which is — you know, when someone’s really good at investing, like they are, and they do something like that, and you look around and see, well, nobody else is really acting in this way — it’s just something that stands out and I think is noteworthy. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So I love the concept of, imagine you only get 20 investment decisions for a lifetime. When you look at Berkshire’s returns, it’s a handful of decisions and decades of sitting still that have been driving it. What is that thesis — hey, you’re only gonna make 20 meaningful investment decisions — what does that do to selectivity? The things that you’re willing to compromise on will — you know, if you need to find a hundred things to own, you gotta make a lot of compromises. If you can own 10 things, you can make less compromises. if you can own one thing, you can get even more selective. I think that idea of knowing what you’re looking for, being patient — and then these two are connected: if you’re gonna act in that way, you have to swing big, to some extent. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So they repeat a lot of the same principles over and over over the years. I’m curious not only how things evolved, but what are some examples of them reaching a conclusion — hey, maybe we haven’t really thought this through, and we wanna pivot or tack away from a previous belief? Where did they really change their minds? One, in an owned business, in GEICO: they basically missed the move in telematics, which is like the data measurement in the car, and Progressive was really early there. Warren publicly, at the meetings, kind of said, we don’t think this is gonna be important to the rate-making decision. they were wrong, and they were years behind. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Explain what telematics does for an insurer. Basically, it gives you actual data from how someone drives, which, it turns out, is very important for determining how they drive and setting their rate and the riskiness, et cetera. GEICO — or the way Warren talked about it, they were convinced— BARRY RITHOLTZ : Is that built into the car, or is it something that you have to give permission for? ALEX MORRIS : You have to get it — you had to get a device at one point. I believe you can do it with your phone now. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And you get a discount if you use it? ALEX MORRIS : You can get a discount for using it. they’ve changed over time what they’re willing to do with your rates, but early on, you could just get a discount from it — you wouldn’t get a rate increase. yeah, Berkshire, or GEICO, kind of missed that early, and they’ve kind of been playing catch-up since then. Progressive went from millions of policyholders less than GEICO to now being quite a bit larger than GEICO. BARRY RITHOLTZ : This is a huge growth story and change for them over the years. Is the telematics strategy what drove them? ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, it’s a huge part of it. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And then the other issue that comes up is that Buffett has been notoriously tech-averse, and then becomes one of the biggest shareholders of Apple. How did he explain that? How did he wrap his head around that major pivot? ALEX MORRIS : That’s the other example I was gonna say. You go through a period of, I believe it’s 2011, 2012, 2013 — some select quotes are, when they owned IBM, they basically said — the person asking the question specifically asked about Apple and Google, which in hindsight is kind of funny, ’cause those are the two companies that they’ve now invested in — they basically said, we’ll never have the confidence in those two companies that we have in IBM. Which was not a good investment. then, I think at the next meeting, Charlie even more forcefully said, basically, Apple’s too hard for us — we’ll never own it. Fast-forward a few years, and I think at one point it was almost a $200 billion position, and it’s one of the greatest investments of all time. I think it just speaks to a willingness to continue learning. you know, Warren specifically talked about, on CNBC when they bought it, how at the Nebraska Furniture Mart — which is a retailer that they own — people come in and buy a TV, and they’re looking at the number of pixels or the quality of the screen, they’re comparing the prices, et cetera. then when it comes to an iPhone versus an Android, it doesn’t matter if an Android phone is 60% cheaper — some people were just absolutely gonna buy the iPhone no matter what. he noticed that, in terms of that differentiation between a technology question versus a consumer brand kind of question. I think he also recognized clearly the value of the screen and the services strategy that Apple, in the mid-2010s, really got underway. the valuation was attractive, and they had a capital returns policy. That’s one of the things that really jumps out in terms of his investment approach: how much he valued, particularly in publicly traded companies, the combination of the valuation and a very clear capital return strategy. You see that at Apple. You see that at PetroChina in the early 2000s. It’s a very prominent part of what he seemed to be looking for. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So I see how their ideas have changed over time. I’m curious — the process of going through the whole book, and all of the various meetings and videos you ended up watching: anything change the way you invest personally? Any ideas you’re still wrestling with, trying to put into practice? I think this idea of — again, I think I mentioned this before — kind of traditional value investors, this idea of change being a bad thing and trying to avoid it. It’s borderline impossible in today’s world. I mean, if you could give me a list of five companies that haven’t meaningfully changed in the last 10 or 15 years, it’d kind of be tough to do. Every industry is changing, and you have to be — you just can’t avoid it. It doesn’t mean you have to run into it, but you have to be really thoughtful about how every business is changing. you think of the prominent examples that they gave over time of, you know, the greatest businesses — newspapers and other things that are either greatly changed or gone. retailers, as an example. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Adapt or die. ALEX MORRIS : Yes, adapt or die. I think that’s a reality of being a business manager. It’s a reality of being an investor. you have to be willing to, you know, lean into that. Coming up, we continue our conversation with Alex Morris, author of “Buffett and Munger Unscripted,” discussing Berkshire Hathaway after Warren Buffett. He is the author of “Buffett and Munger Unscripted: Three Decades of Investment and Business Insights from the Berkshire Hathaway Annual Shareholder Meetings.” He is also the founder of TSOH Research. let’s talk a little bit about their relationship before we get to the post-Buffett — and we’re already in the post-Munger — era. What did Munger contribute to Buffett’s thinking that Buffett probably wouldn’t have developed on his own? They really had kind of a unique partnership. Charlie will say he didn’t have as much of an impact as Warren says he did — so I guess you gotta pick which one you want to agree with or believe. You know, I think Warren’s strategy that he ran up until the point in time when they became friends with each other, and the decades after, was a cigar-butt strategy, a traditional value investing strategy. The main constraint it was gonna run into over time was size — and that’s the problem they have now, even as they’ve adjusted the strategy. I think Charlie changed his mindset a little bit towards buying businesses that they’re gonna own, as opposed to things that are gonna be liquidated or sold, whatever it may be. BARRY RITHOLTZ : When you say buying businesses — completely, like a full takeover? Not just, we don’t want 10% of GEICO, we want all of GEICO? I think one of the prominent early ones was See’s Candies, where they were getting a little touchy on the price, and I think they had someone who worked with them who said, if you guys don’t buy this ’cause the price is 10% higher than what you wanted, you’re idiots, basically. Who says that to Warren Buffett? ALEX MORRIS : I think it was Charlie Munger’s partner — I wanna say Ira Marshall, for some reason, but I could be incorrect. anyways, they told him, if you don’t buy this business ’cause it’s 10% higher than what you want to pay, you’re not being very intelligent, because this is a really good brand and it’s gonna be a really good business over time. BARRY RITHOLTZ : You know, I have a buddy, Jonathan Miller, who’s not only a data junkie with the back end of real estate, an appraiser, but he was saying, if you’re buying a house that you’re gonna live in for 25 years — this is the house — if you pay 10 or 15% over, who cares? Just look at houses sold 25 years ago: what would’ve happened if you paid 10% more for that? Marc Andreessen said the same thing about Facebook. All right, it was a 40x or a 50x — imagine if we paid 25% over. It wouldn’t have made any difference. this is coming from people with a value background. How do you reconcile that? Personally, my personal experience taught me, in some ways, to just get past that way of thinking. again, as I said before, I bought Microsoft in 2011. It was a very traditional value investment — ex-cash, it was trading at a high-single-digit P/E. Again, a very traditional value investment. You get forward to 2015 or 2016, in that period, and now the P/E, as opposed to being in the high single digits, is, call it, mid-teens. I can remember at that point in time, a lot of the, again, more traditional value investors, they were at a point where they’d go, okay, we’ve had our run here — it’s time to sell. It’s a situation where I looked and saw, with Satya Nadella, who was recently named the CEO at that time, the strategy they had in the cloud business — and not that I have any great technical knowledge on this, but the way they explained where they were going and what the opportunity was, it just seemed clear to me that to sell it simply because the P/E was a couple turns higher than, you know, what the quote-unquote fair price was — it just didn’t make a ton of sense. If you’ve found a business that has a really long runway, with a person running it that you think is the right person for that job, to let that go easily is a mistake. it’s funny to look back now — I didn’t know this, ’cause I was updating on Microsoft the other day: over the last decade, the stock’s compounded at a mid-twenties annualized return. ALEX MORRIS : This happens all the time with companies like this, where people, if they become too focused on the valuation, they go, this isn’t gonna generate more than 12% a year over the next decade, or whatever. Price is what you pay, value is what you get. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So clearly, even at an elevated price, Microsoft turned out to be a good value. ALEX MORRIS : You have to consider both at all times. If you become overly focused on price as the driver of your decision-making, I think that’s kind of a flawed way to do things. the same goes for — you know, theoretically, you have a portfolio, and theoretically you could re-rank it every single day on expected five-year returns, whatever it may be, and the answer’s gonna change based on what those positions did the day before. Obviously, I think that mindset, while it makes sense theoretically, guarantees you’re never gonna own anything particularly in size. You’re gonna be trimming it as it goes up 20, 30, 50%, because— BARRY RITHOLTZ : Suddenly it’s fully valued. ALEX MORRIS : The IRR is three points lower than it was six months ago. I just think, if you look back — again, like the last 15, 20 years, and your example of Facebook — selling it because the IRR was down slightly was a mistake, if you understood what the business was, in some sense, and what the opportunity was. Again, you can deal with this through position sizing, but be really thoughtful about selling businesses that you actually think are worth owning. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Yeah, that makes a lot of sense. Both Buffett and Munger have emphasized staying within one’s circle of competence. How can an investor expand that circle, and how do you avoid fooling yourself into thinking you have some competence when you don’t? I think it’s time; it’s a willingness to learn; it’s a willingness to feel around and not always, you know, have the answers right away. I mean, for example, at TSOH, a lot of my initiations on companies — they very rarely end with, you know, this is my price target, or this is a buy today. That’s very uncommon for me. The conclusion is almost always: here’s what I think is interesting about this company; these are the questions we kind of need to explore and get a better feel for over time. it’s just that continual learning process, where sometimes you get, you know, three, four, five years down the road from there and you still don’t have the answers. Other times, you get a couple years down the road and things happen in a certain way, and you go, wait a second — I think I’m seeing this now in a way that I didn’t originally. you find enough examples like that, and you can have a portfolio. What do you think, of all the principles that Buffett and Munger enumerated over the years, are often quoted but really infrequently practiced by professionals, or just difficult to put into effect by mom-and-pop investors? They’ve had things like, you know, permanent capital — which, you look at an example like Terry Smith at Fundsmith right now: when things go against you for a relatively short period of time, but your assets start going away, that’s a huge problem. things like that are just a prominent example of how thoughtfully they’ve constructed everything, and what that then allows them in terms of their flexibility — of, you know, being really patient, or taking big swings, et cetera. BARRY RITHOLTZ : What about “avoid difficult decisions”? ALEX MORRIS : Again, I think it’s more difficult over time. I think if you’re patient, you can — again, as you learn more and more, decisions that may appear difficult might be less so for you. BARRY RITHOLTZ : I really like Buffett’s comment about market forecasts: they tell you nothing about the market, but a great deal about the forecaster. They claim to have never made a Berkshire decision based on a macro prediction. ALEX MORRIS : Well, I think you look at their cash position currently and wonder how much of that is, you know — maybe it’s not a macro forecast, but there has to be some belief about markets or prices generally. I guess you could look at it at a micro level and say, we can’t find anything — and collectively, all the micro is the macro, right? You know, I think the bigger point — and it’s something that we’ve all seen over the past 15 years — I mean, I’m sure you can remember well, 2011, 2012, people were like, okay, we’re back to another bubble; we got past the GFC, and now here we are again, and stocks aren’t gonna go anywhere for the next decade. good call — people who overdosed on that have paid a very significant price. BARRY RITHOLTZ : You know, it’s funny you bring that up. I remember — I don’t remember if it was late ’08 or early ’09, but Buffett wrote an op-ed, I think it was in the Times, “Buy American.” And that felt very much like a combination of, everything has gotten cheaper — so there’s a valuation issue — and, we weren’t quite down 56%, but we were on the way; maybe we were down a third by that time. it felt like a macro call: hey, this is a temporary crisis and we’ll get past it. Or was it strictly a valuation decision? ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, I think it was a little bit of both. I mean, as he said later on — you know, I wrote that in, I think he said, October of ’08, and to your point, people were like, wow, what a great call. It was like, well, it was down another 30% six months later, or whatever it was — so my timing wasn’t particularly great. You know, I think the bigger takeaway, particularly for individual investors, in my mind, is understanding something like a structural asset allocation and having clarity on what you’re trying to achieve. again, coming back to this idea, over and over, of the mistakes you’re trying to avoid. We saw over the past 15 years people making big swings in and outta cash, in and out of the markets. I think you’re just making the game more difficult than it needs to be. when you’re wrong, it really hurts. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So, having studied every answer Buffett ever gave about succession over 31 years, what does the record tell us about how he set up his succession? what did his Thanksgiving letter last year add? ALEX MORRIS : It’s kind of funny — starting with the ’94 meeting, they were asked every single year about succession. BARRY RITHOLTZ : He’s, what — he’s my age back then? He’s in his early sixties back then. It turns out he had another three decades to go. You know, I think they’ve said over time that there’s nobody who cares about the answer to this question more than we do. you know, a lot of the businesses — at BNSF, the railroad, Warren’s not really involved in the decision-making there. Same at GEICO, same at a lot of other businesses. A lot of the equity positions, like I said — Coca-Cola or Amex, all these other ones — they’re just in there, and they’re almost certainly not going to be sold by Warren or anybody else. I think a lot of the pieces are in place. The biggest challenges Berkshire has: as I mentioned, there were some operational issues at businesses like GEICO that had to be fixed, and the massive cash pile is another challenge. Those challenges existed two years ago with Warren, and, you know, they still exist today, and solutions are difficult. it seems like Greg Abel is starting to move in the direction of trying to resolve those issues. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So let’s talk a little bit about Greg Abel. He took over as CEO of Berkshire on January 1st of this year, 2026. You were at the meeting in Omaha, his first annual meeting — Buffett just sitting in the audience like any other Berkshire shareholder. Well, maybe not like any other Berkshire shareholder, but not on stage. Are you confident that this was the right choice and Berkshire is in the right hands? ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, I think that — and this is also informed by writing the book, the questions over time. In the early days, the questions were really focused on Berkshire and investing, and I think as time went on, they became a lot more about life advice and other things that, while still interesting, are not really Berkshire-specific. when you got to things like, as I was saying, GEICO and telematics, or at BNSF, where their results were lagging some of the other Class I rails, I think Warren had a tendency to not wanna point fingers at the managers, and he wouldn’t really talk specifically about the issues there — which, you know, for the people who are kind of the diehard Berkshire shareholders, we want to hear those things. Greg took those questions head-on, which was really refreshing to hear. I think everything we’ve seen so far would suggest that, you know, as Warren and Charlie said, we’ve thought about this more than anyone else — and I think that’s probably reflected in their decision. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So you mentioned the huge cash pile — a couple hundred billion dollars just lying around. I know, that’s walking-around money. What does capital allocation look like under Greg Abel? Is he gonna emphasize buybacks, or going out elephant hunting and finding some big acquisition, or something else entirely? ALEX MORRIS : I think repurchases will surely be a big part of the strategy. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And by the way, Munger and Buffett have both been very explicit about buybacks: hey, when you’re below your true value, when you’re below fair value, it’s a deal — absolutely do buybacks. if you’re fully or richly priced, it’s a disaster waiting to happen. They made no bones about it, and they acted on that. Where do you think Greg falls on that? I think Berkshire started buying shares more significantly — I think they started in 2019. The pace has slowed down lately. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Implying they’re close to fully valued. I believe that they have views about the market, or the opportunity set more broadly — I think that would be fair to say, based on how they’ve been acting for some time now. You know, it would’ve been helpful if they’d started repurchasing shares earlier. I don’t think Warren was particularly interested in doing that for a good amount of time, and it got to a point where they basically had no choice: they either had to, or have to pay a large special dividend, whatever it may be. I think Greg will be a lot more open to leaning into these things. as I said, many times — I mean, obviously we haven’t had huge shakeouts, outside of maybe a brief period during the pandemic, but if we get a period where equities really trade off meaningfully and they can put a decent amount of dollars to work, they’re willing to spend tens and tens of billions of dollars, or potentially even over a hundred billion dollars, if the right opportunity is there. BARRY RITHOLTZ : What’s the cash holdings right now? ALEX MORRIS : I think it’s north of 300. That sounds to me like a war chest waiting for a disaster to happen. I think the thing is, you gotta find a willing seller — which, if you’re gonna buy a whole business— BARRY RITHOLTZ : Do you have to find a willing seller, or can you wait for an era of distress, where everybody’s a seller and you are the — well, you know. That’s what I meant by war chest waiting for disaster to strike. ALEX MORRIS : Well, that’d be a nice way to deal with this issue. we haven’t seen it yet, but I’m sure the day will come where things look really ugly, and I’m sure they’ll be ready to act — and will act. BARRY RITHOLTZ : So the whole idea of the annual meeting taking place in Omaha was really built around these two men, Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger — one of whom is no longer with us, and the other one is now sitting in the audience. the question that comes to mind is, does Omaha still matter today? What’s it gonna look like, you know, a decade from now? It’s funny — I think, and I’d say from my experience here, and from people I know who are also Berkshire shareholders, it sounds like their experience has been similar — it’s become an event where, you know, people go there, and there’s so many events around the meeting now that aren’t the meeting. It’s people coming together who are hosting their own meetings of one variety or another, or having investor conferences. yeah, I think that’s become a really important part of this trip for a lot of people. I sense — I mean, the size of the audience will get smaller, as it has already, I believe. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Oh, is that true? ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, I think it was smaller this year than it’s been in the past. for the core group of, you know, the diehard value investors, I think they’ll continue to show up for a while, as long as those events keep going on. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Do you have any insight into who the average Berkshire shareholder is? Is this primarily Main Street, or is this more professional investors, or some obvious combination? ALEX MORRIS : Yeah, I think it’s a combo of the two. It feels like a combo of the two. They definitely attract a more Main Street audience than, I think, just investors do generally — or investment managers, especially. BARRY RITHOLTZ : And I’ve never made it out to Omaha. I’m curious — who goes to these events? ALEX MORRIS : Value weirdos. People always like to joke that, you know, “I’m a contrarian” — and I’m sitting in here with 40,000 people who think the same way I do. BARRY RITHOLTZ : It’s the scene from Monty Python’s Life of Brian. ALEX MORRIS : Yes, exactly. BARRY RITHOLTZ : You’re all individuals — you don’t have to follow the crowd. they just repeat in unison, “We’re all individuals.” ALEX MORRIS : No, I think it’s people who wanna learn. for myself, it’s — you know, I’ve learned a ton from Warren and Charlie about business, but I’ve learned a lot more as well about life and other things that I think are, you know, as important as part of your development as an individual and as an investor. it’s funny — I wrote Warren in 2010, and I said, hey, I’m not asking you for a job, and I have fantastic parents who are my role models, but outside of that, you’ve been really important to my life, and I just wanna say thank you for that. he wrote a response, and it’s framed in my office. It’s probably the one material possession that I care about. you know, I think it’s people with that mindset, who have come to really appreciate all they’ve taught people. obviously, Warren, through charity and other things, has done a lot for the world at large as well. I only have you for so much time, and we don’t have the studio for so much time, so let’s jump to our favorite questions that I ask all of my guests — starting with, and I kind of have a suspicion as to the answer of this: who were your mentors who helped shape your career? I know you have the letter from Buffett, so I want you to address Buffett and Munger, as well as anybody else who might have shaped the curve of your career. ALEX MORRIS : My start was with Peter Lynch, actually. ALEX MORRIS : I think “One Up on Wall Street” was one of the first books I read, which, even to this day, when younger people ask me what should I read, I think that’s a perfect book for getting a feel for what investing is, and it’s very approachable. I’ve always liked Peter Lynch. Other investors like Chuck Akre and some of these other fund managers — Ackman’s another example — fund managers, at least in the early 2010s, were names in the world that I tracked, and they were well known and people that I learned a lot from. Obviously, Warren and Charlie are at the top of that mountain for me. BARRY RITHOLTZ : Let’s talk about books. What are some of your favorites, and what are you reading currently? ALEX MORRIS : Currently reading the Jeremy Grantham book, which I thought is an interesting book.

items.summary: 8月25日，Apple公司更新了妙控鍵盤的細節外觀，按鍵Tab、Caps Lock、Shift、Return和Delete等鍵帽不再使用文字標識，而是改為⇥、⇪、⇧、↵、⌫等純符號標識。同時，帶數字鍵盤的妙控鍵盤也將Home、End、Page Down、Page Up等鍵帽改成了純符號標識。本次更新的產品有妙控鍵盤、帶觸控ID的妙控鍵盤，以及帶觸控ID和數字鍵盤的妙控鍵盤（白色、黑色），唯一沒有更新的是無觸控ID帶數字鍵盤的妙控鍵盤。OpenAI釋出ChatGPT Admin外掛8月26日，OpenAI公司推出了一款全新的ChatGPT Admin外掛，讓工作區管理員可以直接透過對話管理使用者和許可權、分析使用情況，並根據相關資料生成報告。透過Admin外掛，管理員可以直接在ChatGPT Work和Codex中完成日常管理工作。管理員可以檢視ChatGPT Work和Codex的活動資料及額度使用情況，找出哪些團隊可能需要進一步支援，並及時發現哪些成員或團隊即將達到額度上限。管理員可以新增或移除成員、調整群組設定，並處理常規的入職、離職以及團隊變動等事務。管理員還能夠檢視使用者的實際許可權，排查訪問問題，並根據角色或群組控制不同功能和模型的訪問許可權。管理員可以調整個人、群組以及整個工作區的額度限制，根據當前使用情況稽核相關申請，並在掌握完整背景資訊的情況下批准或拒絕這些請求。近日，為慶祝寶可夢誕生三十週年，閃迪公司推出了兩款授權儲存產品，分別是閃迪寶可夢USB-C快閃記憶體盤夢幻版和閃迪寶可夢行動式SSD超夢版。兩款產品分別採用夢幻和超夢主題設計，在便攜儲存之外加入更適合粉絲和收藏者的外觀元素。其中超夢版行動式SSD從超夢的力量感汲取設計靈感，最高讀取速度為1000MB/s，效能最高可達傳統行動式硬碟的五倍。產品還具備最高兩米的跌落防護，適合儲存和處理照片、影片等體積較大的檔案；容量可選500GB和1TB，售價分別為119.99美元和199.99美元。夢幻版USB-C快閃記憶體盤採用小巧的口袋式設計，最高提供128GB容量。產品支援相容的手機、平板電腦和電腦，方便使用者在不同裝置之間儲存、傳輸和讀取照片、影片及其它日常檔案。多親於8月26日釋出一款多親J36 AI按鍵智慧手機，定價659元。多親J36搭載2.8英寸480*640解析度螢幕、MTK8766V處理器、3GB + 32GB儲存、2600mAh電池，執行Android 13系統。內建的QIN AI支援一句話開啟藍芽、一句話撥打電話、一句話完成AI寫作。軟體功能上，支援微信、支付寶、音樂、影片等各種app，家長可審批安裝、遠端禁用、管理時長等；有攝像頭版本配備13MP後置+ 2MP前置攝像頭，無攝像頭版本背面取消了鏡頭模組。Commodore推出《賽博朋克2077》主題復古電腦8月26日，Commodore團隊聯合CD PROJEKT RED，為旗下Commodore 77復古電腦推出一款《賽博朋克2077》主題特別版，這是Commodore品牌歷史上首次推出基於遊戲IP打造的聯名硬體，目前已經開啟預訂，售價377美元，明年年初發貨。該產品以Commodore 64 Ultimate為基礎，採用《賽博朋克2077》風格半透明菸灰色機身，帶有金屬銘牌及青綠色氛圍燈，機身底座同時還擁有可隨音樂變化的LED燈效。Commodore 77還提供大量《賽博朋克2077》主題元素，包括定製版Commodore 77 BASIC 2.0開機介面、新選單配色、霓虹電源燈、貼紙、徽章、主題包裝，以及包含遊戲世界觀資料和《賽博朋克2077》主題BASIC程式的定製螺旋裝訂說明書。同時，該產品還附帶一款專屬DEMO演示程式，由波蘭C64 DEMO團隊Arise製作，並由晶片音樂製作人LukHash創作原聲，該DEMO卡帶僅隨Commodore 77附贈。硬體方面，Commodore 77本質上是一款基於FPGA技術打造的Commodore 64復刻版復古電腦，主要用於玩Commodore 64遊戲。相比原版Commodore 64的約1MHz處理器，新機最高執行頻率提升至77MHz，並採用AMD Artix XC7A100T FPGA，效能強於Commodore 64 Ultimate使用的XC7A50T。8月26日，微軟公司釋出部落格文章，回顧了過去一年Windows on Arm平臺取得的重大進展。微軟表示，很高興看到英偉達將於今年晚些時候憑藉RTX Spark SoC加入Windows on Arm陣營，與高通驍龍X平臺一道，進一步鞏固Windows on Arm平臺的發展前景。尤其是到了2026年秋季，微軟Surface、華碩、戴爾、惠普、聯想和微星都將推出搭載RTX Spark的裝置。微軟還重點介紹了目前已經登陸Arm平臺的Windows應用，包括STEM（科學、技術、工程和數學）及教育類應用、安全應用、生產力應用、創意類應用以及娛樂和媒體應用等。目前已經支援Windows on Arm的應用包括ShareX、Proton Mail、Signal、Discord、FxSound等。微軟稱，目前Works on WOA網站已經收錄並追蹤超過七千款相容Windows on Arm的應用，並推薦該網站作為查詢應用相容性資訊的綜合性來源。微軟表示Windows on Arm如今已經不再只是一個充滿潛力的平臺，而是正在快速擴大的生態系統，擁有不斷增加的裝置，並覆蓋客戶最依賴的各種工作場景和應用。隨著開發者持續投入Arm原生體驗和相容性開發，消費者在選擇下一代Windows裝置時將擁有更多選擇、更大的靈活性，也會更加有信心。

items.title: 輝達員工果斷出手 50 坪大宅！力麗關係企業力銘建設首案落腳北士科
items.summary: 力麗集團關係企業力銘建設董事長郭淑珍今日表示，未來十年將以雙北蛋黃區為唯一戰場，預計採「都更危老整合」與「素地購置」雙軌並進，目前已完成13案布局，土地儲備逾9,300坪，推估總銷規模上看千億元，首案「力銘耘山」落腳北士科，並透露已有輝達員工果斷出手50坪大宅。郭淑珍表示，台北市已進入沒有素地的時代，未來能買到素地當然買，買不到就一塊一塊整合，力銘建設未來十年的開發總銷規模上看千億元，但千億並不是業績目標，而是一份責任，力銘建設這兩年已在雙北市心完成13案土地布局，其中12案坐落台北市。郭淑珍指出，力銘建設未來將以雙北蛋黃區為唯一戰場，預計採「都更危老整合」與「素地購置」雙軌並進，首案「力銘耘山」落腳北士科輝達特區，總銷65億元，預計2030年落成，目標與輝達（NVIDIA）總部「星群」同年啟用，成為台灣AI核心區重點地標。力銘建設不做郊區，未來十年只做一件事，郭淑珍指出，那就是在雙北最難取得土地的精華地段，蓋出數十年後依然亮眼的建築，並替北市高齡化住宅存量提出解方，因此「力銘耘山」特地請來國家金獎大師李天鐸操刀。海悅總經理王俊傑表示，輝達年初與北市府完成T17、T18基地簽約，權利金122億元，設定地上權50+20年，投資總額逾400億元，規劃容納約4,000名員工，加計金仁寶、康舒進駐，全區預估帶動近6萬個就業機會，但住宅用地僅13.8%，顯示土地供給與人口導入呈現高度落差。王俊傑指出，北市科最大的市場優勢在於「供需極度不平衡」，園區未來預計將湧入超過6萬名就業人口，但純住宅區的土地面積極小，依照目前市場評估，未來北市科的新案總供給量僅約1,500戶，這在未來龐大的潛在需求面前顯得杯水車薪。王俊傑強調，這批高資產買方具備雄厚財力，鎖定台北市地段優越、具獨特性的物件，面對總價超過7,000萬元的標的，多半不需依賴貸款即可成交，但這類客群並非盲目追高，而是在購屋前做足功課，一旦確認物件符合需求，出手十分果斷。「力銘耘山」距輝達總部約650公尺，規劃地上18層、地下5層，總計102戶，郭淑珍指出，目前已銷售三成，其中有四成來自科技業，並有輝達員工果斷出手，原以為會鎖定小坪數，結果當天就直接購買50坪以上大宅，顯示具備強大資產實力的買方對北市科未來發展深具信心。郭淑珍強調，「力銘」是取自父親郭木生事業版圖「力」麗集團，以及家族早期發跡的「銘」隆布行，代表要時刻提醒自己不忘本心，並計畫未來每年穩健推出1~2案，而「力銘耘山」作為力銘建設第一個里程碑，更將為城市留有深刻美學記憶。 請參閱所附表格 ↛

items.title: 彭博經濟學家：下週非農恐再轉負，連兩月負增長 Fed 沒升過息
items.summary: 彭博經濟研究首席美國經濟學家Anna Wong發文指出，下週五（9/4）公布的美國8月非農就業報告有相當機率再度負增長，而現代聯準會歷史上，沒有在非農連兩月負增長時升息的先例。此說出現在Fed主席Kevin Warsh傑克森霍爾放鷹、9月升息機率單日從35.4%跳到55.7%之後。本文歷史數據由動區動趨依美國勞工統計局發布日程與FRED資料庫核算整理。彭博首席美國經濟學家Anna Wong稱8月非農可能負增長，市場共識是正9至11萬人FRED資料核算：1954年來連兩月非農轉負共20次，其後三個月升息的只有2次Kevin Warsh放鷹後，CME 9月升息機率從35.4%跳到55.7%，比特幣跌破78,000美元下週五（9/4）公布的美國8月非農就業報告，可能不是市場想的那樣。彭博經濟研究首席美國經濟學家Anna Wong發文指出，這份報告有相當機率再次出現負增長。FactSet調查的預估中位數是新增11萬人，凱投宏觀（Capital Economics）估9萬人，失業率維持4.2%。Anna Wong的說法等於在講，這些數字可能全部押錯方向。如果8月真的轉負，那就是連續兩個月負增長，而現代聯準會歷史上，沒有在這種情況下升息的先例。美國7月非農減少23,000人，是今年2月以來首度轉負。當時市場預期是增加8萬人。5月與6月合計被下修103,000人。原本以為還在長的兩個月，其實長得比帳面少很多。時薪年增率則是3.2%。動區用聖路易聯準銀行FRED資料庫的原始就業序列核對過，7月與6月的全美非農就業人數差距，正好就是減少23,000人。連兩月轉負的20次裡，只有2次後面是升息Anna Wong說的「沒有先例」到底有多硬，可以自己算。以有效聯邦基金利率有紀錄的1954年7月為起點，美國非農就業連續兩個月負增長的獨立事件總共出現20次。把每次事件成立後三個月內的有效聯邦基金利率月均值拿來比，上行超過1碼（25個基點）的只有2次。那2次是1954年7月和1957年6月，都落在1950年代。那個年代聯準會還沒有現在的目標區間框架，利率本來就跟著資金市場浮動，很難算是政策決定要升息。1957年10月之後的18次，一次升息都沒有，全部是持平或往下走。這18次涵蓋1974年石油危機、2001年網路泡沫、2008年金融海嘯，還有2020年疫情。8月28日，聯準會主席Kevin Warsh在傑克森霍爾（Jackson Hole）年會首度以主席身分發表演說，調性偏鷹。他表示近期通膨數據還不足以證明價格壓力真的降下來，並重申2%通膨目標「不可動搖、也不容談判」。路透引述的CME FedWatch數據顯示，9月升息機率從週四的35.4%跳到55.7%。目前聯邦基金利率目標區間是3.50%到3.75%，9月FOMC的開會日期落在15日到16日。美國勞工統計局定在9月4日美東時間上午8點30分發布，台北時間為當晚8點30分。市場共識預估新增9萬到11萬人，失業率維持在4.2%。依FRED資料核算，1954年以來共20次連兩月非農轉負，其後三個月有效聯邦基金利率上行超過1碼的只有2次，都在1950年代，之後18次全是持平或降息。

items.title: 少人知道的烏俄戰爭秘密：普丁把 600 年前聖人遺骨送上前線，想靠超自然力量扭轉戰局
items.summary: 普丁在8月20日走進克里姆林宮天使長主教座堂，在一具打開的白石棺旁點了根蠟燭。棺裡是14世紀莫斯科大公德米特里頓斯科伊的遺骨，7月修教堂時挖出來的。他稱這個發現是「奇蹟」，並批准俄羅斯東正教會把骨頭分裝進聖物匣，送往烏克蘭前線鼓舞士氣。前兩批都沒能撐住，最近一批在7月中旬被無人機炸毀，隨行3名軍官陣亡。普丁8月20日視察克里姆林宮出土遺骨，批准教會把碎片送往烏克蘭前線鼓舞士氣這是第三批送上戰場的聖髑，涅夫斯基那批7月中旬遭無人機炸毀，3名軍官陣亡俄科院院士承認DNA未能證明身份，教會仍在8月18日宣布確認為頓斯科伊他手裡拿著一根蠟燭，站到一具打開的白色石棺旁邊，聽專家解釋裡面那副骨頭是誰的，然後他舉起手畫了十字。克里姆林宮發布的影片裡出現了祈禱儀式，祈禱的對象寫得很清楚：常勝的軍隊、俄羅斯民族，以及總統本人。儀式結束，普丁走過去查看兩具打開的墓。14世紀的莫斯科大公，1380年在庫利科沃戰場擊敗蒙古金帳汗國，1389年過世時39歲，在1988年時因為受洗千年，他被俄羅斯東正教會封為聖人。這副聖人骨頭是7月教堂搶修時，在南牆下的地下室挖出來的。保存得幾乎完整，只缺一塊左腳跟骨。聖人的骨骸又叫做「聖髑」，屬於聖物的一種。挖到的位置本身就出乎意料。歷史學家原本認為頓斯科伊葬在教堂的另一側，石棺卻出現在南牆底下。牧首基里爾已經下令把遺骨切分，裝進聖物匣。其中一份要送到烏克蘭前線，讓俄軍的官兵們瞻仰。教會與社會及媒體關係部門副主任Vakhtang Kipshidze說得很明白，應該盡快讓官兵有機會朝拜，把聖髑送進作戰區是鼓舞士氣適當的做法，普丁在教堂裡點頭了。這是2026年，戰爭用AI和無人機在打的時代，聖物、宗教、超自然力量還被投入戰爭。兩個月前，俄羅斯國防部長Andrei Belousov才公開說，俄軍正在把人工智慧、機器人與自動化指揮系統整合進部隊管理。去年4月，普丁本人在軍工委員會上講過一句話：誰更快在軍事上用上AI，誰就能在戰場上取得巨大的優勢。今年5月他還說，全世界只有三個國家有能力開發主權AI，俄羅斯是其中之一。現在俄國正在研究怎麼把一副637年前的骨頭安全運到頓內茨克。上一具聖髑，在半路被無人機炸掉了這不是俄羅斯第一次把聖人遺骨送上戰場。涅夫斯基的部分聖髑被送往前線，提議的人就是國防部長Belousov。夏天開始，這批聖髑被用在祈禱儀式上，祈求解決燃料危機，特別是恢復克里米亞的供油。7月中旬，官兵用卡車把它運往頓內茨克一處重要設施，準備再辦一場祈禱。聖髑全毀，3名軍官當場死亡。前一年，莫斯科的聖馬特羅娜聖髑也被送到前線，毀於砲擊。根據Nasha Niva引述的消息，俄國防部內部開始擔心Belousov跟基里爾牧首之間會鬧翻。一名國防部消息人士的說法是這樣的：我們相信，儘管如此，新的聖物還是會抵達前線。教會自己公布三年來的「戰爭成績單」是在前線為42000名士兵施洗、蓋了140座野戰教堂、派出2,000名神父。2024年，世界俄羅斯人民大會通過的文件正式把這場戰爭定義為「聖戰」。8月18日，俄羅斯東正教會宣布鑑定完成，這副骨頭確認屬於頓斯科伊。幾天後，俄羅斯科學院考古研究所主任、院士Nikolai Makarov對外說明鑑定過程。他的原話是，DNA分析做了，樣本也採了，但「沒有提供關於德米特里教會的認定靠的是另一套：遺骨屬於一名身高不到180公分的男性，35到45歲之間，死於自然原因。教會的結論是，這些特徵「與關於大公生平與死亡的書面史料和歷史證詞相符」。這是「不排除」，不是「確認」。頓斯科伊39歲過世，剛好落在35到45這個區間。但符合這個區間的中世紀莫斯科貴族男性，不會只有他一個。Makarov提到，俄國實驗室已經復原了部分前蒙古時期留里克王朝成員的遺傳特徵，理論上可以拿來比對。俄羅斯記者Ksenia Luchenko的判斷更直接。她說這件事明顯「不是即興的」，準備了相當長一段時間。歷史學家跟教會本來就知道頓斯科伊葬在哪裡，要做的只是把墓打開。也許當局需要另一個神秘主義兼意識形態的事件，因為動能正在消退。普丁自己在教堂裡的說法也不像臨時起意。他說，我昨天跟聖下談過，知道他的計畫，請代我向他致意。拿聖物去影響戰爭結果，20世紀有過更有名的版本。1938年3月德奧合併之後，同年10月13日，哈布斯堡王朝的帝國御寶在黨衛軍押送下從維也納運到紐倫堡，存放在聖凱瑟琳教堂。御寶裡有一件「聖矛」，傳說是羅馬士兵朗基努斯刺進耶穌肋旁的那把矛，後來被叫做「命運之矛」。這裡要講清楚，希特勒癡迷這把矛的超自然力量，這個說法主要來自1973年英國作家Trevor Ravenscroft的暢銷書《命運之矛》。歷史學界普遍認為，那本書把史實、民間傳說跟作者自己的神秘主義詮釋混在一起。真正查得到的只有兩件事，矛被納粹搬走了，1946年由美軍歸還維也納。希特勒的超自然故事是戰後別人替他寫出來的，而且被史家質疑了半個世紀。烏克蘭的回應來得很快，8月22日，外長Andrii Sybiha在基輔與德國外長Johann Wadephul的聯合記者會上被問到這件事。普丁已經開始訴諸一些奇怪、滑稽的東西，他們把德米特里我們的立場是，既然普丁是和平的唯一障礙，他不如跟這具骨骸換個位置。意思就是說，普丁可以自己躺在棺材裡當具死人骨頭，不得不說這句話回擊相當有力。要知道，烏克蘭的主要宗教天主教和俄國信的同個上帝，只是有些地方出身的聖人，似乎永遠都無法安息。14世紀莫斯科大公，1380年在庫利科沃擊敗蒙古金帳汗國，1389年39歲過世，1988年被封聖。他是「以弱擊強、擊退外敵」的象徵，蘇聯在二戰時也用過同一個名字募款造坦克。俄科院考古研究所主任Nikolai Makarov說DNA分析做了，但「沒有提供關於德米特里教會的依據是身高不到180公分、35至45歲自然死亡、與史料吻合，屬於不排除而非直接證明。

items.title: 比特大陸推出兩款水冷礦機 S23 XP Hyd、S23e U2H
items.summary: 比特大陸在8月27至28日於香港舉行的世界數位挖礦峰會（WDMS）上發表兩款水冷礦機：旗艦S23 XP Hyd算力600 TH/s、能耗比8.9 J/T，整機期貨價15,300美元，最快11月交付；2U機架式的S23e U2H算力865 TH/s，促銷價9,515美元，鎖定標準IDC機房改造。旗艦S23 XP Hyd：600 TH/s、8.9 J/T，期貨價15,300美元，11月起交付以現價自算：U2H回本約14個月，旗艦近兩年半，買的是能耗比生存力礦機龍頭比特大陸8月27至28日在香港瑰麗酒店舉辦年度世界數位挖礦峰會（WDMS），一口氣發表兩款水冷礦機。今年峰會主題就叫「Ride the Cycle. Hydro Prevails.」，直譯是「駕馭週期，水冷當家」，新品全部走水冷路線。旗艦款Antminer S23 XP Hyd算力600 TH/s，能耗比8.9 J/T，整機功耗5,340W。期貨單價25.5美元/T，一整台15,300美元，預計2026年11月至2027年1月交付。另一款S23e U2H走完全不同的路線。它是2U機架式水冷機，算力865 TH/s、能耗比10 J/T，促銷單價11美元/T，整機9,515美元，設計目標是塞進標準IDC機櫃改造的機房。一台賣效率，一台賣「裝得進資料中心」，兩款機器瞄準的是兩種完全不同的買家。旗艦賣效率，比去年進步6%去年同一場峰會發表的S23 Hyd，算力580 TH/s、能耗比9.5 J/T；今年旗艦推進到600 TH/s、8.9 J/T，能耗比進步約6%。8.9 J/T是什麼概念，就是挖出同樣的算力，電表走得比去年慢6%。對電費佔營運成本大宗的礦場來說，能耗比每降0.1，關機價就往下挪一格，熊市裡能撐得比別人久。現在下單付的是期貨價，機器最快11月才到手，買家等於押注三個月後的難度與幣價。U2H賣的是「伺服器適用規格」2U機架式代表它跟一般伺服器同一種尺寸規格，鎖定的是用標準IDC機櫃改造的機房，而不是傳統礦場的貨架。礦企正在把機房轉租給AI，Riot Platforms 8月才簽下98億美元的AI資料中心長約。機房規格向資料中心看齊之後，同一批基礎設施今天可以放礦機，明天可以換AI伺服器，資產不會被挖礦用途鎖死。以比特幣現價約77,600美元、全網算力約857 EH/s、電價每度0.06美元估算（不計難度變動），S23 XP Hyd一天約可挖0.000315枚BTC，收益約24.4美元，扣掉約7.7美元電費，日毛利約16.8美元，回本要接近兩年半。S23e U2H一天收益約35.2美元，扣約12.5美元電費，日毛利約22.8美元，回本約14個月。S23 XP Hyd是比特大陸2026年WDMS峰會發表的旗艦水冷礦機，算力600 TH/s、能耗比8.9 J/T、整機功耗5,340W，期貨單價25.5美元/T（整機15,300美元），預計2026年11月至2027年1月交付。S23e U2H是2U機架式水冷礦機，尺寸規格與一般伺服器相同，可裝進標準IDC機櫃改造的機房。算力865 TH/s、能耗比10 J/T、功耗約8,650W，促銷價11美元/T，整機9,515美元。

items.title: 聖結石宣布復出！是因為加密貨幣漲了嗎？
items.summary: 百萬YouTuber聖結石8月28日發片宣告回歸，理由是太太生病求醫三年、接著育兒三年，今年4月請到家庭幫傭才擠出時間。面對「是不是虧太多才復出」的質疑，他回「工作賺錢天經地義，沒人嫌錢多」。不過動區查了他的頻道紀錄，那支影片不是他今年的第一支，他從6月4日就開始發片，累積15支，而比特幣這波反彈是最近一個月的事。動區查核其頻道RSS，他從6月4日就開始發片、至今15支，最高一支10萬觀看，8月28日那支是說明片不是第一支比特幣近30天漲21.29%，但近一年仍跌29.62%、距2025年10月高點126,080美元還差38.5%百萬YouTuber聖結石8月28日發了一支影片，片名前半是他的招牌台詞「我BANG回來了」，後半接著問「我復出的真正原因其實是⋯？」，到29日中午累積6萬多次觀看。他自己給的答案跟幣圈無關，他說停更不是過氣，是「真的沒時間」，太太嘟嘟生病四處求醫花了三年，接著懷孕到全職帶小孩又三年。今年4月申請到外籍家庭幫傭，晚上才終於擠得出空檔。復出的契機他形容是「全憑運氣、半推半就」。原本為了研究AI應用去碰TikTok，不小心按到直播，老粉一擁而上；後來直播裡喊經典台詞「Bang」，加上PK輸掉喝香菜奶茶的懲罰片段在IG Reels破百萬觀看，才接到大學校唱和遊戲主題曲的邀約。這句話沒有否認什麼，也沒有承認什麼，跟我差不多。頻道紀錄跟「停更六年」對不上8月28日那支不是他今年的第一支影片，而是第15支。他從6月4日就開始發，6月三支、7月四支、8月七支，8月28日一天發了兩支。中間觀看數最高的是7月11日那支「音樂課本出現我？再往前拉，他的長片列表在那支之前是五個月前，再往前就直接跳到三年前的一整排。所以「停更六年」是他自己算的人生階段，三年陪病加三年育兒，跟頻道的更新紀錄是兩件事。以長片來說停了大約三年，而短影音早在兩個多月前就回來了。回到社群的猜測，比特幣現在報77,555美元，近30天漲了21.29%，這波反彈是真的有點感覺。比特幣近一年跌29.62%，距離2025年10月6日創下的126,080美元高點還差38.5%。以太幣更明顯，現在2,435美元，近一年跌44.56%，離2025年8月的高點腰斬一半。他6月4日開始發片的時候，這波反彈根本還沒發生。要說幣漲了所以他回來，日期擺在一起就不成立。聖結石本名曾聖傑，2016年10月開始經營個人頻道並每日發片，用225天衝破百萬訂閱，是當時台灣最快的紀錄，這個紀錄到2025年3月才被Andy老師打破。2021年底他發行個人名義的NFT，首發售罄，也推廣了台灣項目甜園狗Sweetyard Dog，還說過自己在2022年第一週靠NFT賺了上千萬。2022年3月，甜園狗地板價從0.3 ETH崩到0.01 ETH、代幣SYD跌掉96.13%，他清空IG與YouTube，被網友罵「割韭菜、高歌離席」。他當時發文說自己沒烙跑，刪貼文是在看心靈類書籍想追求清淨，並承諾「未來關於幣圈的話題我會更謹言慎行」。2024年7月受訪時，他說自己從1萬台幣開始投資，最多時接近一半資產在加密貨幣，但當年4月就把本金全部贖回，剩下的持倉全是淨利。2025年1月捲入蔡阿嘎前員工的租屋爭議時，他自我介紹的身分是全職投資者，做天使投資與新創孵化。照他自己講過的版本，本金早在兩年前就抽回來了，這輪跌價傷不到他的成本。真要說這次復出被什麼推了一把，比較可能的答案是香菜奶茶。

items.title: 冰島「重啟入歐」公投開票：Yes 微幅領先，牽動漁業主權與克朗換歐元命運
items.summary: 冰島8月29日公投是否重啟中斷13年的歐盟入盟談判，目前開票Yes以51.17%些微領先No的48.83%，牽動40萬人口小國的克朗是否讓位歐元。8月29日公投決定是否重啟中斷13年的歐盟入盟談判，目前開票近尾聲，Yes陣營以51.17%些微領先No的48.83%，已計104,731張有效票，結果要等冰島時間週日中午才明朗。對這個人口不到40萬的島國來說，公投答案未來將決定克朗是否讓位給歐元、8%高利率能不能壓下來，以及漁業主權要不要交給布魯塞爾。選前民調早在誤差範圍內拉鋸：Maskína民調51.3%支援、48.7%反對，週五另一份則是Yes 50.4%。」，這是諮詢性公投，Yes過關不代表入盟，後續還要再辦一次公投、經國會透過、修憲，並經歐盟27國簽署。13年前喊卡的談判，這次能重啟到哪一步？冰島入盟故事得從2008年金融危機說起：銀行體系崩潰後，雷克雅維克2009年啟動入盟談判，2013年喊停。喊停前已有進展，35個章節中27章啟動、11章暫時完成，歐盟理事會紀錄顯示，執委會官員評估剩餘進度可在1到2年內完成。冰島早已透過歐洲經濟區身分加入單一市場與申根區，正式入盟只是再往前一步，一併帶進關稅同盟、最終走向歐元。No陣營的焦慮不是安全，而是飯碗：漁業與海洋產業佔冰島出口近4成。反對黨主席Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir直言，這不是在問要不要跟歐洲合作，而是冰島人是否願意把漁業、農業與自然資源的決策權交給布魯塞爾。歐盟共同漁業政策讓No陣營寢食難安，誓言不與他人分享水域；許多冰島人忘不了1970年代打贏英國的「鱈魚戰爭」，漁業向來是入盟辯論的最大主因。Bifröst大學教授Eirikur Bergmann告訴BBC，冰島是歐洲最富裕國家之一，「很多人把這歸功於獨立」。獨立克朗讓冰島能自訂利率、用匯率吸收衝擊，2008崩盤後與觀光、漁業收入起伏時都證明過價值；代價是利率卡在7.5%到8%，通膨達5.6%，冰島工會調查稱冰島是全球物價最貴的國家。總理Kristrún Frostadóttir投票後說這是勢均力敵的競賽，「非常刺激」，並強調Yes不代表入盟，若No勝出會尊重結果。若Yes勝出，談判最快2026年底啟動，耗時18到24個月，談成還要再辦一次公投；No勝出則政府承諾2028年前不重啟，是否撤回申請交由國會決定。冰島是北約創始成員卻沒有軍隊，防務須靠盟邦，1951年起與美國有雙邊防務協定；同時俄烏戰爭也讓冰島對俄羅斯在附近海域的動作提高警戒，讓外界憂心川普對接管格陵蘭的野心，他甚至把格陵蘭跟冰島搞混過。今年歐盟與冰島簽署安全與防務夥伴協議，官員稱這是「價值、繁榮與安全共同體的錨」。

items.title: 兩大音樂巨頭 Sony、Warner 控告 Anthropic 大規模非法下載：一首歌最高求償 15 萬美元
items.summary: 兩大音樂版權巨頭以「大規模非法下載」為由，將Anthropic與兩位創辦人一併列為被告，求償門檻直指美國聯邦法院。美國聯邦法院不久前才替AI訓練畫出一條界線：用受版權保護的作品訓練模型本身不違法；現在Sony Music Publishing與Warner Chappell這兩家音樂版權巨頭，就把這條界線寫進了對Anthropic的訴狀裡。兩家公司本週已在美國加州北區聯邦地方法院提告，把Anthropic公司本身、執行長Dario Amodei、共同創辦人Benjamin Mann一併列為被告。原告在訴狀裡，把這起案件形容為「史上規模最大、最明目張膽的智慧財產竊盜案之一」，求償金額上看數億美元。這份48頁的訴狀裡，原告指控Anthropic「以龐大規模，非法透過BT種子下載、大量爬取網路資料的方式」，取得數以萬計的詞曲版權作品，藉此開發、營運並從Claude系列AI模型獲取巨額利潤。訴狀還指出，Anthropic曾從MusixMatch、LyricFind等已取得授權的歌詞資料庫爬取內容，並主張先前在UMG、Concord、ABKCO一案後加上的防護機制，只要重新下一次提示詞就能輕易繞過。原告要求陪審團審理，每件「故意侵權」的作品最高可求償15萬美元的法定賠償金，每移除一次著作權管理資訊（CMI，也就是歌曲裡標註創作者與版權歸屬的資料），再加碼求償最高2.5萬美元。相較於BMG先前對Anthropic提告時只鎖定493首歌曲，Sony與Warner這次涵蓋的作品數量是「數以萬計」，範圍寬得多。這也不是音樂版權方第一次對Anthropic出手：今年1月，另一批版權方才剛提告，一次涵蓋逾2萬首歌，求償金額超過30億美元。這場官司之所以特別燙手，先要理解一個容易被忽略的細節：Sony Music Publishing與Warner Chappell這兩家公司，管的是「詞曲版權」，也就是作詞作曲的創作權利，而不是「錄音版權」，也就是母帶錄音本身的權利。這場官司背後真正的主體，是音樂出版商，而非唱片公司。這個區分很重要，因為它代表Sony Music、Warner Music旗下的唱片公司，未來還能就同一批訓練資料，以錄音版權為由另外再告一次，等於同一批歌曲，有機會被拆成兩條戰線，各自求償。一首歌能拆成好幾塊各自獨立的版權：歌詞、母帶錄音、詞曲創作，分別握在不同的權利人手中，可能是歌手、出版商，也可能是唱片公司。凡是正式發行、需要個別授權的商業歌曲，都能讓原告有很強的立足點去主張法定賠償金，而法定賠償金最大的好處是，原告不必在法庭上證明自己實際虧損多少錢，只要證明侵權事實成立，賠償金額就照法律規定的上限計算。同一首歌只要背後牽涉的權利人夠多，理論上可以被拆成好幾張告訴狀，分別求償，數字乘起來，遠比單一著作權訴訟可怕。2025年9月，Anthropic才與作家、出版商達成一項15億美元的和解，創下美國史上最大宗著作權和解紀錄。當時主審法官的判斷邏輯很清楚：拿受版權保護的書籍訓練模型本身合法，但透過盜版管道下載這些書，不合法。Sony與Warner這次的訴狀，幾乎是把同一套邏輯原封不動搬到音樂產業，只是把「書」換成了「歌」，而音樂版權因為權利人分散、單曲數量龐大，一旦法院採信，潛在的賠償金乘出來的數字，可能比書籍案更誇張。把訴訟壓力從公司資產負債表，推到創辦人個人身上，這種寫法在AI版權戰場上並不常見，某種程度上也是一種施壓訊號，等於告訴外界：這不只是公司決策的錯，是有人親自拍板的結果。Axios媒體記者Sara Fischer分析指出，音樂版權結構性的複雜，恰好讓AI公司暴露在多重訴訟風險之下，同一首歌可能同時面對來自作詞人、唱片公司、出版商的個別求償。音樂產業對著作權議題向來出了名地愛打官司，經歷過Napster、LimeWire年代的人都清楚這一點。面對指控，Anthropic對此回應：「我們不認同版權方的主張，並打算在法庭上積極為自己辯護。它真正劃出的戰線，不是AI能不能拿受版權保護的作品訓練模型，而是每一家AI公司，都得回頭交代清楚，自己當初的訓練資料究竟是怎麼來的。

items.title: 比特幣礦企 IREN 的 AI 收入首超挖礦！但財報淨虧 6.84 億美元，股價大跌超 12%
items.summary: IREN最新財報跨過一個關鍵里程碑，AI雲端收入7,050萬美元首次超越比特幣挖礦收入，但也同步交出6.84億美元淨虧損與4.5億美元裝置減值。短期轉型成本沉重，但40億美元簽約營收隱含2026年的爆發潛力。挖礦巨頭IREN最新財報跨過一個關鍵里程碑：AI雲端收入7,050萬美元，首次超越比特幣挖礦收入6,670萬美元。但淨虧損6.84億美元，股價收盤重挫12.53%，反映市場對短期轉型成本的謹慎。AI收入超越挖礦，財報資料「好看但不美」-總營收：1.372億美元，季減5%、年減85%AI雲端收入：7,050萬美元，季增一倍以上、佔總營收51.4%比特幣挖礦收入：6,670萬美元，季減40%、佔總營收48.6%Adjusted EBITDA：1,920萬美元，季減68%、年減93%非現金減值：4.504億美元，主因挖礦裝置退役AI收入超越挖礦是象徵性分水嶺，但財報整體呈現「收入結構改善、獲利能力倒退」的矛盾狀態。轉型成本：裝置退役+人力擴張雙重出血IREN正在把原本用於挖礦的資料中心改裝為AI算力基礎設施。-裝置減值：4.5億美元非現金減值，來自退役的比特幣礦機資產人力成本：AI雲端營運需要更多工程與售後團隊，薪資支出大幅攀升資本支出：AI晶片、冷卻系統、電力升級需要持續投資，但營收需等客戶上線後才逐步認列這解釋了為何EBITDA暴跌68%。轉型期是「先花錢、後收錢」的結構性虧損。40億簽約營收vs 10億營運，隱含爆發潛力IREN在財報中指出，2026年容量已繫結40億美元的年化常態營收合約，但目前僅10億美元處於營運狀態。這是典型的SaaS/雲端營收認列模式：合約先簽、營收按月認列。如果2026年能順利把更多容量上線，AI雲端營收有望從7,050萬美元一季，逐步逼近年化40億美元的上限。市場反應：股價跌12%看什麼？挖礦收入季減40%，傳統現金流正在流失30億未營運合約存在交付風險（工期延誤、客戶退約、AI需求降溫）IREN正處於「舊引擎熄滅、新引擎還在暖機」的真空期。IREN的故事能否說通，關鍵在接下來幾個季度的三個指標：-容量上線速度：10億→ 40億的爬坡曲線，能看出交付執行力EBITDA觸底回升：當AI收入規模效應展開，人力與裝置成本攤薄，獲利應能改善客戶名單：合約背後的客戶是誰，直接影響收入可持續性如果2026年下半年IREN能證明「AI雲端不只是故事、而是真現金流」，那這次的6.84億虧損只會被視為轉型必要的過渡成本。

items.title: Polygon 悄悄硬分叉堵 3 個漏洞：修復 DoS 攻擊風險與驗證者資源耗盡
items.summary: Polygon透過Austin和Kyoto兩次硬分叉修復Bor與Heimdall客戶端的3項漏洞，包含DoS攻擊風險與驗證者資源耗盡，官方表示漏洞未遭主網利用。Polygon實驗室在官方論壇公布，近期透過兩場硬分叉修復了影響Polygon PoS網路的數項安全漏洞，涵蓋拒絕服務（DoS）攻擊風險、驗證者資源耗盡，以及checkpoint與milestone處理缺陷。3項漏洞詳情：Heimdall最嚴重，Bor有2項DoS風險根據Polygon Labs驗證者支援團隊在論壇的公告，漏洞影響Bor與Heimdall兩個核心客戶端：- Heimdall嚴重級：攻擊者可透過精心設計的transaction，迫使驗證者執行大量運算工作，進而幹擾網路正常運作。Bor DoS風險（1）：可放慢區塊處理速度。Bor DoS風險（2）：可導致節點當機。Polygon強調，上述漏洞「均未在主網被觀察到遭利用」，修復是預防性部署，細節公開前補丁已上線。兩場硬分叉採「私密部署+測試後上主網」模式：- Austin HF：對應Bor v2.10.0，所有Polygon PoS節點皆需升級。Kyoto HF：對應Heimdall v0.11.0，驗證者與全節點皆需升級。公告指出，硬分叉啟用高度（activation heights）透過後，未升級的舊版客戶端已失去共識權，必須更新才能重新接回主鏈。「先修後說」是常態，但這次涉及DoS風險Polygon此次選擇在補丁上線後才公開漏洞細節，這在區塊鏈資安圈是標準做法，避免駭客在升級完成前利用未補漏洞。類似策略在以太坊、Cosmos、Solana等生態皆常見。- Heimdall的資源耗盡漏洞屬於理論上可導致網路停擺的等級。Bor的DoS風險直接影響出塊效率，若被惡意利用，可能導致Gas費飆升、交易延遲。對比Polygon歷史上多次因漏洞導致網路停機（2021年12月240億美元漏洞、2025年Bor節點bug分叉），這次「未遭利用就補完」算是處理得相當及時。POL價格反應平淡，月漲44%仍跑贏大盤訊息公布後，POL（前身為MATIC）價格波動有限。年內至今（YTD）：漲2.3%市場對Polygon PoS的關注焦點仍在其與zkEVM生態的整合進度，以及Layer 2競爭格局下的定位。此次資安修復雖未觸發恐慌，但也反映出Polygon基礎設施仍在持續面臨技術挑戰。-驗證者升級率：雖然未升級節點已掉線，但需確認所有主要驗證者都已完成升級，避免共識分歧風險。Polygon漏洞揭露透明度：Polygon Labs是否會建立更系統化的漏洞披露機制（如CVE編號、定期資安報告），讓生態開發者能更即時掌握風險。在Layer 2競爭白熱化的環境下，基礎設施的穩定性與透明度，是Polygon能否留住開發者與機構使用者的關鍵。
